title: Egypt’s reopening of its embassy in Tripoli signals regional shift on Libya
excerpt:
The reopening of the Egyptian embassy in Tripoli marks a fundamental political shift, both domestically and regionally, for Libya, analysts say.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty inaugurated t...
body_text:
The reopening of the Egyptian embassy in Tripoli marks a fundamental political shift, both domestically and regionally, for Libya, analysts say.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty inaugurated the historic embassy building on Saturday, which had been closed for 12 years due to security concerns.

Libya has been politically divided since the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, with rival administrations formed in Tripoli in the west and Tobruk and Benghazi in the east.

Egypt was widely considered to be backing the eastern authority, effectively led by strongman and renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, and his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), until recent regional developments led Cairo to rethink its approach.

Libyan political analyst Hazem al-Rayes said the reopening of the embassy in Tripoli – which was the seat of the internationally recognised government that Haftar was fighting – is a sign of this.

“I can consider that what Egypt is doing in its recent moves towards the capital, Tripoli, is an attempt to readjust its behaviour in the Libyan file … [for] five years, no Egyptian foreign minister visited the capital,” he told Al Jazeera.

Elias al-Barouni, a political science professor at Libya’s Nalut University, also believes the move goes beyond the resumption of regular consular services in Tripoli.

“We are facing an indicator of a shift in Cairo’s method of managing its relations with the Libyan parties, and a rearrangement of its priorities in dealing with the Libyan crisis,” al-Barouni told Al Jazeera.

There have been several significant political and regional shifts that have somewhat stabilised the volatile situation in Libya, where thousands have been killed in fighting between militias attached to rival political authorities.

In July 2026, Ankara and the LNA reached unprecedented coordination, spearheading agreements to develop military facilities, advanced surveillance systems, and training programmes in Turkiye for eastern Libyan officers.

The deputy commander of eastern Libyan forces and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, has also paid visits to regional capitals, including Turkiye and Qatar, which have supported the United Nations-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) in Tripoli.

In Libya, rivals recently signed the so-called “4+4 agreement” that sets out a roadmap for possible presidential and legislative elections over the next two years.

Badr Hassan al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution at Cairo University, told Al Jazeera that Egypt came to revisit its policy towards Libya after realising that its reliance on eastern forces, led by Haftar, was not conducive to its overall strategic interests.

“It is clear that Cairo … found that relying on one party or leaning towards one party in Libya, which is Haftar’s party, may not be the right bet perhaps at the present time or even for a while, since the Turkish intervention several years ago,” al-Shafei told Al Jazeera.

“Consequently, perhaps Egypt wants to create a balance or also send a message to Haftar that he should not act unilaterally and that acting should be in coordination with Cairo, so it worked to extend bridges of cooperation with Libya also …”

Egypt has also become more concerned about developments to the south of its border, particularly the expansion of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, which had allegedly received support from Haftar.

“Today, Egypt is no longer the Egypt of five years ago when its policies and relations were limited only to the [eastern] authorities in Benghazi,” al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

It is “convinced today that its ally [LNA], which it supported throughout the past years at the expense of the legitimate government in Tripoli … has distanced itself from it today, and it needs to readjust its political behaviour with Tripoli and with the legitimate government”, he said.

During Abdelatty’s visit to Tripoli, he discussed critical economic files with Libyan officials, including the 2019 maritime border memorandum of understanding signed between Tripoli and Ankara.

According to the Facebook page of the Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Abdelatty reaffirmed the importance of addressing Egyptian concerns regarding maritime demarcation between Libya and Turkiye in light of international law. The eastern parliament recently ratified the maritime agreement, which it initially opposed.

“Consequently, perhaps Cairo is trying to prevent the ratification of this agreement from causing damage to its interests in gas and oil exploration in the Eastern Mediterranean, and from that it wanted to extend bridges to Tripoli as well,” al-Shafei said.

“Instead of limiting itself to political and diplomatic objection from outside Tripoli, Cairo has become negotiating directly with the Libyan government that signed the agreement.”

Egypt might also be attracted to opportunities that reconstruction and the revival of Libya’s oil industry might bring.

“Perhaps with the reconstruction process, the incoming Egyptian labour will have priority, or even the currently present one will have its living conditions improved, not to mention the idea of the possibility of Egyptian investments and companies entering the reconstruction process,” al-Shafei said.

After years of backing rival sides, a new regional consensus means there is a greater likelihood of rivals in Libya reaching a comprehensive agreement to end the war, al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

But al-Barouni cautioned that there is still a plethora of issues facing Libya, and only a comprehensive solution can end the divisions within Libya.

“The Libyan problem is not merely a dispute over the name of the head of government, but rather it is a dispute over the nature of power, the distribution of influence, control over institutions and resources, the future of the military institution, and the conditions for reaching elections,” al-Barouni said.

“If Cairo, Ankara, Washington, and other capitals agree on the necessity of ending the division, that is a development that can be built upon, but the success of any settlement remains linked to the ability of the Libyans to formulate an independent national project. Libya needs a settlement that ends the division, not a deal that redistributes the division.”

title: DAVID MARCUS: How Ashley Moody survived the blue tsunami and emerged as a GOP star.
excerpt: Bold conservative policies and crucial ballot measures helped Florida successfully mitigate the blue 'wave' during the midterm elections. Governor Ron DeSantis discusses how his state avoided a near e...
body_text:
Bold conservative policies and crucial ballot measures helped Florida successfully mitigate the blue 'wave' during the midterm elections. Governor Ron DeSantis discusses how his state avoided a near extinction level event for the Republican Party.

Even in the face of massive losses in last week’s Midterm elections, Republicans had a few winners, and none may have longer-lasting effects than Sen. Ashley Moody of Florida who defied national trends for a GOP hold in the Sunshine State.

Going into Tuesday’s contests, holding a Senate seat in Florida may have seemed like the least Republicans could do, but it turned out to be a night where the least they could do was the most they did, and those who did win should be learned from.

"I fought tooth and nail this election to make sure Floridians know that what we have here is special, and it can be dismantled in one cycle," Moody told Fox News Digital in the wake of the blue tsunami, and while that message faltered in states like Texas, in Florida it stuck.

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

Moody said her campaign held to two basic messages.

"Talking to folks on the ground and meeting them where they were was vital, and I heard many people from all political backgrounds present a consistent message – they want a government that is accountable and a government that protects their pursuit of the American Dream. I put that front and center in my campaign and Floridians backed me for it."

Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., departs the Senate Chamber at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, June 4, 2026. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Accountability and the American dream: These are two very good places to start as the GOP licks its wounds and seeks a path back to power on Capitol Hill having squandered both houses in this cycle.

DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED

Many have been tempted to dismiss Moody’s victory by saying, "but it's red Florida." But red Texas turned bluer than the Gulf of America. So no, Florida did not carry Ashley Moody. Ashley Moody helped carry Florida.

Moody was twice elected statewide as attorney general, first in 2018 by low single digits, then in 2022 by a whopping 21% of the vote, and unlike Ken Paxton, the Texas AG who lost his Senate bid last week, Moody did not have a long resume of scandal to bog her down.

Moody also outperformed South Carolina Sen. Darlene Graham, who took over the seat of her late brother Lindsey Graham after he died earlier this year, a decision driven by President Donald Trump that many believe cost Republicans the Palmetto state seat.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton addresses supporters at Federal American Grill in Houston during his "Come and Take It" bus tour ahead of the midterm election against Democrat James Talarico, Oct. 30, 2026. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Now, in the new Congress, Republicans will end up having lost between seven and nine seats. What this means for Moody is a fast track to seniority. With GOP Senate stalwarts like John Cornyn of Texas and Susan Collins of Maine having lost this cycle, Moody has jumped significantly ahead in line.

MASSIVE UPSET: ANDREWS DOWNS TRUMP-BACKED GRAHAM IN RUBY-RED SOUTH CAROLINA

Although Moody is just as much responsible for Republican success in Florida - which also included the election of Rep. Byron Donalds as governor - as Republican success in Florida is for Moody, one would be remiss not to mention current Gov. Ron DeSantis, the architect of the so-called ‘free state of Florida."

DeSantis has built a GOP brand in Florida that is laser focused on the two issues Moody credited for her victory, government accountability and saving the American dream for the next generation.

DeSantis made his state a beacon for conservatives across America who came in droves from places like New York City, now, it may become a lighthouse, guiding a national Republican Party adrift at sea back to the shores of electoral victory.

Of the GOP wipeout, DeSantis said, "A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate. That’s just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn’t deliver it."

This is noticeably at odds with Vice President JD Vance’s theory of the loss, which states that GOP voters did in fact come out, but voted for Democrats, mainly because of the war in Iran and our nation’s relationship with Israel.

Figuring out which of these theories is true, or at least dominant, is the first order of business for Republicans looking to regroup, and it is worth noting that while the GOP lost Vance’s old Senate seat in Ohio, Moody held Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Florida seat intact.

Vance and DeSantis may get the chance to pitch their visions of the GOP to Americans over the next two years in a presidential primary race, but in the meantime, the biggest Republican winner of the Midterm debacle is Ashley Moody, who suddenly looks like a force in American politics that we should all get used to.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DAVID MARCUS

David Marcus is a columnist living in West Virginia and the author of "Charade: The COVID Lies That Crushed A Nation."

title: Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says
excerpt:
High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels

The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can s...
body_text:
High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels

The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.

The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”

Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”

Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”

But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.

The summit will have a notable absentee, with the US refusing to send a delegation for the second year in a row. The Trump administration wants no part of “extremist climate policies” embraced by other countries, according to a White House spokesperson.

Donald Trump expressed glee shortly before the US midterm elections about the huge profits made by oil and gas companies due to the Iran war, which he started and has caused an increase in living costs around the world. “I don’t give a damn,” the president said at a recent rally in Georgia. “I’m going to say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune.”

However, a group of 20 Democratic members of Congress have made the trip to Antalya, buoyed by their party’s stunning success in the US midterms last week that will enable them to stymie Trump’s attempts to dismantle pollution rules and withhold financial support for clean energy.

Developing countries and civil society will seek to put climate finance and justice at the heart of the Cop31 talks. Rukiya Khamis, the east Africa programme manager at the 350.org campaigning group, said: “Across east Africa, people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. From prolonged droughts to destructive floods, we are losing homes, livelihoods and access to food and water. Yet the money needed to respond to these impacts remains out of reach for many of the countries and communities most affected. It is fundamentally unjust that those least responsible are being left to carry the greatest costs.”

This summer more than 50,000 people died in Europe due to heatwaves, severe wildfire smoke shrouded swathes of North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal triggered a landslide that caused more than 1,500 deaths, while the El Niño weather event, described as “staggering” by scientists and still to reach its peak, is gathering strength.

However, while the pace of progress on cutting global emissions has been slow, the Iran war has spurred many countries to see fossil fuels as expensive and vulnerable to shocks, while renewables continue to plummet in price.

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said before the talks: “Climate impacts hit every population and every economy harder each year. [But] almost every major economy, and many medium-sized and smaller economies, now see climate action as a central driver of economic growth, jobs, and affordable and secure energy.”

Cop host Turkey also wants more countries to switch to electric technologies, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, as these are many times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts. A target for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035 will be on the table, but faces opposition from some.

Both presidency countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Australia is one of the world’s leading exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas. The centre-left Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and have more than 80% of its electricity generated by solar and wind by 2030, but is off track to meet them.

Labor also faces a political threat from the resurgent rightwing One Nation party, which dismisses climate science. One Nation and the Liberal and National party coalition want to scrap the net zero goal.

The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “This summer, we all felt it: climate change is here, in Britain, now. No country can tackle it alone, which is why Cop31 matters. The answer to high bills and climate change is the same – more clean, homegrown power, creating good jobs and warmer homes. Cop31 is about Britain’s national interest.”

title: Women in media alleging abuse too often not protected, Lisa Nandy says
excerpt:
Culture secretary says there is still a problem in the industry and public life after Russell Brand conviction

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said there is still a problem with exploitation a...
body_text:
Culture secretary says there is still a problem in the industry and public life after Russell Brand conviction

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said there is still a problem with exploitation and abuse in the media industry and a failure to properly deal with allegations after Russell Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault.

She said women who came forward were too often not protected by institutions across public life, including in politics, and that huge power imbalances meant speaking up came at a very heavy cost.

Nandy told the media industry that “time is up” to bring in systems to protect vulnerable whistleblowers, and said that while the BBC had taken action in recent years, other organisations still had to take the issue seriously.

Brand’s conviction on Thursday renewed scrutiny of how the UK’s entertainment industry has treated celebrities accused of abusing their power, with some women saying they feared that speaking out could harm their careers.

Brand faces sentencing on Monday after being found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others.

Nandy said last week that the case must be a wake-up call to the media world and beyond, after widespread concerns over failures to confront Brand’s behaviour. It emerged after the verdicts that he is under investigation for two further rape allegations.

In an interview with the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy was asked whether she thought there was still a problem in the media and creative industries. “Yes, I do, and I think hand on heart I can’t say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is,” she said.

“The biggest reason I say that, and I won’t say it lightly, is because I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse. I think they’re not protected.

“I think that they work in industries like politics and media where the power imbalances are huge, where they’re often on short-term flexible contracts, and where who you know and reputation is often the key to career advancement. Speaking up has a very heavy cost.”

She praised the BBC for signing up to the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority, a whistleblowing body, and for taking other steps in recent years, but she said there was more the corporation could do.

“There are other institutions that haven’t done that, and time is up,” she said. “It really is time for the media industry to take this seriously and to put those practices into action.”

Nandy had said earlier on Sky News Sunday Morning that the government was considering what further steps it could take to help protect whistleblowers in such circumstances.

title: Houston Texans and Los Angeles Chargers meet in a matchup of two surprisingly struggling NFL teams
excerpt: The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-7, and Nick Wright has called them the "biggest disappointment in NFL history." Chris Broussard and Kevin Wildes discuss this take and ask if it’s valid, and they discus...
body_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-7, and Nick Wright has called them the "biggest disappointment in NFL history." Chris Broussard and Kevin Wildes discuss this take and ask if it’s valid, and they discuss Shedeur Sanders being in line to start for the Cleveland Browns as Deshaun Watson is in concussion protocol.

Being an NFL schedule maker can’t possibly be an easy job. Obviously, the logistics will be a challenge no matter what season you’re trying to prepare. Stadiums are used for a lot of things, and planning for events and games can’t be easy. Sometimes they provide flex schedule games so that they can put bigger and better games in prime spots.

However, things also sometimes happen when two expectedly good teams end up bad, like today’s game between the Houston Texans and the Los Angeles Chargers.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Houston Texans come into this game with a 2-5 record, but if you’re going to pick either of these two teams to make the postseason, it is hard to pick against Houston. The Texans came in with a defense that was expected to be one of the best in the league. Houston has a young defense, but they are allowing 24.3 points per game. Their passing defense has been awful this season, allowing 244.0 yards per game. To make it even worse, they’ve faced about half good and half bad quarterbacks.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

C.J. Stroud of the Houston Texans looks to pass the ball against the Kansas City Chiefs during the third quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on Dec. 7, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Jamie Squire/Getty Images)

Sure, they faced Josh Allen and Joe Burrow in the first two weeks. They also faced Dak Prescott in Week 4 of the season. However, they’ve also faced Daniel Jones, Cam Ward, and JJ McCarthy. They played Trevor Lawrence in London as well. It just doesn’t seem to add up why they are struggling so much this season. The offense isn’t giving them much to work with. They have the fourth-worst running game in football, but they have one of the best passing offenses.

The Los Angeles Chargers are not going to make the postseason, and honestly, they are probably closer to blowing up the team than they are to anything else. This has been the biggest disaster, and, arguably, the most confusing team of the entire season. The Chargers are 0-7 to start the season, and even a Bye Week didn’t help them get ready enough for last week. Their offense has been terrible; their defense hasn’t been impressive.

Justin Herbert of the Los Angeles Chargers throws a pass in the first quarter against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, Tennessee, on Nov. 2, 2025. (Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images)

Justin Herbert, a guy that people expected to be among the best in the league with new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniels, has regressed significantly. Herbert has five touchdown passes and 10 interceptions this season. He hasn’t thrown a touchdown pass in the past two games, but has completed three passes to the other team. The Chargers are going on 10 straight quarters without a touchdown. They’ve only scored a touchdown in one of the past 12 quarters they’ve played. It has been embarrassing.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel and Justin Herbert of the Los Angeles Chargers look on before a preseason game against the San Francisco 49ers at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., on Aug. 20, 2026. (Getty Images)

I think this game is likely to be a bit higher scoring than what we see on the total of 40.5. The Texans can put up 20+ points against the Chargers. Los Angeles hasn’t scored, but for whatever reason, the Texans can’t really stop anyone. I think Los Angeles might even win this game, but backing them is scary. I’m going to take the over 40.5 here. Eventually, we will see something out of the offense, and I think the Texans will do enough. Give me the over.

title: Chicago Bears favored by six as Tampa Bay Buccaneers try to keep their division hopes alive
excerpt: After the Chicago Bears beat the Seattle Seahawks, there is now a massive shakeup in Danny Parkins’ Top Ten teams in the NFL, including the Jacksonville Jaguars as well. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, ...
body_text:
After the Chicago Bears beat the Seattle Seahawks, there is now a massive shakeup in Danny Parkins’ Top Ten teams in the NFL, including the Jacksonville Jaguars as well. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes join to ask what kind of statement the Bears made with this win.

Primetime games almost always have better match-ups. I’m fairly certain every NFL team is given at least one primetime game each season. However, some teams have significantly more games in the Primetime window than others. The Bears, who play tonight on Sunday Night Football, are one of those teams, and they are playing in their third straight primetime slot. The Buccaneers haven’t had as many primetime games, but this could be a good one either way.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers come into this game with a 3-5 record and are coming off one of the most interesting wins of the entire season. They shut out the Falcons and won 16-0, but that isn’t even the most unique part of the victory. It was that they won the game without completing a pass. It was very rainy, but the team only attempted three passes all game. The team ran the ball 56 times – 52 if you only include the running backs. Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell combined for 310 rushing yards.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers running back Bucky Irving celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys in the first half of an NFL football game in Arlington, Texas, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Julio Cortez)

The rest of the season hasn’t been overly impressive, but they have won three of the past four games. They beat Dallas by eight points behind their backup quarterback. They lost to the Steelers in overtime, and it was unfortunate because they were winning almost the entire game. They destroyed the Panthers, and then they beat the Falcons. It was a rough start to the season, but their division isn’t very good, so maybe they still have a chance to win it.

TAMPA BAY BUCCANEERS WIN NFL GAME WITHOUT COMPLETING A PASS, FIRST TIME THAT'S HAPPENED IN HALF A CENTURY

I guess I should start with an apology to the Chicago Bears. They are better than I expected and better than I gave them credit for. I had a lot of questions about if their team had actually won any impressive games. My conclusion was… not really. Last week, they played a great game against a very good Seattle team. Their offense was strong behind a great running game and timely passes. Best of all, a delay-of-game penalty actually saved the Bears. They had the penalty and then threw a 30+ yards screen pass the next play that set up a touchdown.

BEARS PROVE THEY ARE NFC NORTH'S MOST COMPLETE TEAM WITH COMMANDING WIN OVER SEAHAWKS

Chicago Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons (99) leaves the field after the Bears defeated the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field in Seattle, Wash., on Nov. 2, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The Bears kind of went all in last week. They traded for Jeffery Simmons to shore up their defense, and he was instantly an impact on the team. He had six tackles and a sack. What it really did was open up some other guys to get in on the action and give more pressure. Simmons was doubled most of the night, and he looked great. It was impressive that Simmons was putting that much energy and effort into the game. I think he can be a real difference maker, and if he keeps it up, Chicago won’t miss the picks it gave up for him.

Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) looks to pass with pressure from Pittsburgh Steelers linebacker T.J. Watt (90) during the first half of an NFL football game Sunday, Nov. 23, 2025, in Chicago. (AP Photo/Nam Huh)

I’ve always thought draft picks were a bit overrated in football, but because of the salary cap, I do understand the extra value. The Bears are playing good football, and the Buccaneers are starting to turn it around. The weather won’t be great for the game, but it should be good enough for the teams to score. I like the over, but I prefer to take the Bears -6. I think Tampa will struggle against Simmons and Montez Sweat. Give me the Bears, but I would also advise taking them in a teaser.

title: Could Iraq’s Kurdish region return to two separate administrations?
excerpt: Disagreements between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) over the formation of a new government have led to the threat of two rival administrations emergin...
body_text:
Disagreements between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) over the formation of a new government have led to the threat of two rival administrations emerging in the Kurdish region of northern Iraq, analysts say.

The dispute between the two dominant political forces in the semiautonomous Kurdistan Regional Government, which traditionally has operated under a power-sharing agreement, escalated after a parliamentary session was held last week in Erbil without the PUK’s participation.

PUK leader Bafel Talabani responded by withdrawing his party from the government, and a threat is growing that a rival administration could be formed in the party’s Sulaimaniyah base.

Independent Kurdish politician Yasin Aziz said the latest developments have deepened the historical divisions between the KDP and PUK.

“I believe the spectre of two administrations in Kurdistan is now very close, and the outlines of such a scenario are becoming clear. … The events have been painful and rapid. The differences between the two parties were significant and have now led to a breakdown in relations,” Aziz told Al Jazeera.

“There had been hopes that the two sides would reach an agreement, but activating parliament without the PUK deepened the divisions between the KDP and PUK.”

The KDP, which is led by Massoud Barzani, is the biggest party in the region, and its strongholds are in Erbil and Dohuk.

Since the first Gulf War in 1990 and 1991 and the establishment of a US-led “no-fly zone” in northern Iraq, Iraq’s Kurds have largely governed themselves, separate from the national government in Baghdad.

The Iraqi Constitution enacted after the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq recognised the northern Kurdish region as a federal entity with its own legislative, executive and judicial powers.

There is a historical precedent for the possible separation of powers in this region between two rival authorities. When a conflict erupted between elements of the KDP and PUK in the 1990s, the two parties formed separate local governments in Erbil and Sulaimaniyah, respectively.

While there have been no recent violent flare-ups between the two parties, political distrust remains deep.

During the sixth parliamentary elections in the region on October 20, 2024, the KDP won 39 seats and the PUK 23. This left a 16-seat gap between the two parties.

But the KDP’s ability to form a new government was still dependent on reaching an agreement with the PUK and other parties, such as the New Generation Movement, which secured 15 seats in the last election.

The PUK has so far refused to collaborate, so after a two-year wait, the KDP reactivated the regional parliament on Wednesday without its rivals.

Although the rivalry between the two parties is longstanding, Aziz argued that the current crisis is more serious and deeply rooted than previous political disputes.

“Given the political stubbornness of both parties, I do not expect an agreement or understanding to be reached soon,” he said. “Both sides must make concessions to each other. The party willing to make greater concessions will demonstrate greater concern for the Kurdistan region.”

Aziz was clear in laying blame for the deepening divide.

“The responsibility for deepening this conflict lies with the leaderships of Kurdistan’s two main parties,” he said. “Their failure to recognise the risks posed by continuing these disputes is one of the reasons we have reached this point.”

Subhi Mandalawi, a member of the KDP, blamed the current impasse on the refusal of the PUK to form a new government with the KDP.

“Following the Kurdistan parliamentary elections, the PUK delayed the formation of the new government. They were counting on the KDP being unable to secure the legal quorum needed to convene a parliamentary session,” Mandalawi told Al Jazeera. “But we held a parliamentary session without the PUK in 2018 as well, and they subsequently joined the government and parliament.”

Mandalawi insisted that the door remains open for the PUK and other political parties but warned that prolonged divisions would lead to deeper problems for the Kurdish region.

“Continuing to obstruct legislative institutions two years after the elections is unacceptable and harms the Kurdistan region domestically, regionally and internationally,” he said.

“Threatening to divide the Kurdistan region is a hasty, ill-considered and unrealistic decision. No party leader can take such a step, and the PUK would be the biggest loser if it went ahead with it.”

Despite the differences, there is little risk of a return to conflict between the two parties. “We are brothers, and there can be no fighting among us,” Mandalawi said.

Mahmood Khoshnaw, a senior PUK official, said the KDP’s decision to convene parliament without his party has worsened political tensions in the region.

“Activating parliament without the PUK represents a departure from the principle of partnership and from political realities, and there will be consequences. If a prime minister is appointed in Erbil, we will take the same step in Sulaimaniyah. Whatever the KDP does, we will do the same in Sulaimaniyah,” Khoshnaw warned.

“The situation in the Kurdistan region is heading towards chaos unless the crisis is addressed rationally and realistically. Activating parliament without reaching an understanding with the PUK has had a negative impact on relations between the two parties.”

Despite this, there are questions about whether Sulaimaniyah could legally separate from the Kurdish regional government.

Ramadan Albadran, an independent political analyst and constitutional affairs expert, said the dispute is not a constitutional issue about the KDP’s convening of parliament but a deep political crisis with the potential to create security repercussions for the region.

The Iraqi constitution also provides no mechanism for dividing the region into zones of influence between the KDP and PUK.

“If the PUK moves to separate Sulaimaniyah from the Kurdistan region, that would not be a legal or constitutional act,” Albadran said.

“If it takes place without a mandate from the elected Kurdistan Regional Government, it would be closer to an act of rebellion since there is no legal provision permitting withdrawal from or the dismantling of a region in this manner.”

title: Second world war veterans outnumber former PMs for possible last time on Remembrance Sunday
excerpt:
Andy Burnham takes part at Cenotaph in London for first time alongside eight ex-premiers and 12 second world war veterans

Second world war veterans outnumbered former prime ministers for what could b...
body_text:
Andy Burnham takes part at Cenotaph in London for first time alongside eight ex-premiers and 12 second world war veterans

Second world war veterans outnumbered former prime ministers for what could be the last time at the national service of remembrance at the Cenotaph in central London.

The number of veterans from that conflict attending the service has dwindled to about a dozen, the oldest of whom was Jeffrey Brereton who served in the RAF. He volunteered for the air force in 1940, at the age of 19, and served as a mechanic on Hurricane aircraft during the Battle of Britain.

The number of former prime ministers has swelled to nine, all of whom attended as Andy Burnham took part in the ceremony for the first time. They included John Major, 83, the oldest living former prime minister; Keir Starmer, the most recent ex-premier; and Liz Truss, the shortest-serving.

Some of the spouses of former prime ministers joined Burnham’s wife Marie-France van Heel on a balcony overlooking Whitehall. She was flanked by Victoria Starmer and Hugh O’Leary, Truss’s husband; Theresa’s May’s husband, Philip; Gordon Brown’s wife, Sarah, and Rishi Sunak’s wife, Akshata Murty.

Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, laid a wreath for the first time. Only leaders whose parties hold six seats or more are entitled to take part, and over the last year defections from the Conservatives have taken Reform beyond that threshold to eight MPs.

Other politicians who laid wreaths included Kemi Badenoch, Ed Davey, Shabana Mahmood and Lindsay Hoyle.

The first wreath was laid by King Charles, who was dressed in a field marshal’s uniform. He was joined by his son, William, wearing the black uniform of a lieutenant colonel of the Household Cavalry.

Minutes before the ceremony, one of the soldiers in the parade on Whitehall was taken away on a stretcher after fainting. Charles led the two-minute silence which was broken only by a crying baby in Whitehall.

A gun was fired to mark the end of the silence before the Last Post was sounded by the buglers of the Royal Marines. After the service about 10,000 veterans took part in a march-past with more than 300 different armed forces and civilian organisations represented.

Some veterans waved and saluted as they began the march after the wreath-laying ceremony. Some of the older members were in wheelchairs and one group, many of whom were adorned with medals, rode mobility scooters.

They were applauded by the crowd as they marched swiftly through Whitehall. The youngest taking part was eight-year-old Ronan Doncaster, who walked in honour of his father: a guardsman with the 1st Battalion Coldstream Guards who died in April 2024.

In Enniskillen in Northern Ireland, the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, and the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, attended a memorial service. In 1987, the event was targeted by an IRA bomb that killed 11 people on the day and a 12th victim, who never woke up from a coma, years later.

In Scotland, the first minister, John Swinney, led tributes at a service outside Edinburgh City Chambers. A military parade marched down the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle, led by the RAF Central Scotland Pipes and Drums.

A service attended by veterans, faith leaders and representatives of the armed forces was also held in George Square, Glasgow, with a silence at 11am followed by a wreath-laying ceremony.

title: MICHAEL GUILLEN: Science's fantastic discoveries are making religion more credible
excerpt:
Former NASA astronaut Barry ‘Butch’ Wilmore discusses the agency's updated Artemis timeline and challenges of returning astronauts to the moon.

I’ll never forget the time I received my very own micro...
body_text:
Former NASA astronaut Barry ‘Butch’ Wilmore discusses the agency's updated Artemis timeline and challenges of returning astronauts to the moon.

I’ll never forget the time I received my very own microscope for Christmas; suddenly, a drop of pond water became a teeming cosmos of strange, wriggling creatures. Nor will I ever forget peering through my first telescope; suddenly, the moon’s eerie, cratered surface exploded to life and looked close enough for me to touch.

Those two boyhood experiences tell the entire, exciting, unexpected story of science in a nutshell. With every new, more powerful imaging device, scientists have gradually, spectacularly brought to light the once-shrouded secrets of the microscopic and macroscopic cosmos.

Throughout this long, impressive eye-opening drama, scientists have justifiably boasted about how their discoveries are systematically ridding our species of its hoary, benighted superstitions, religion included. This conceit is displayed in the title of Carl Sagan’s book The Demon-Haunted World: Science As a Candle in the Dark. For Carl — a professor of mine at Cornell — science was indeed the great, bright hope for a terribly dim-witted world.

NASA'S CHANDRA TELESCOPE REVEALS MILKY WAY'S OUTER REACHES MAY STRETCH FARTHER THAN PREVIOUSLY KNOWN

But, the story of science hasn’t turned out as the optimists prophesied, not by a long shot. That’s because modern science is discovering there’s far, far more to reality than meets the eye, than even our most sensitive instruments can see. That we live in a demon-haunted cosmos after all — one infested with invisible, inscrutable spirits with such names as dark matter and dark energy.

As a grad student at Cornell, I recall learning about what my astronomy professors called the "missing mass problem," a mystery dating back to 1933, when Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky used data from Mount Wilson Observatory’s powerful Hooker telescope to study clusters of galaxies. To his astonishment, Zwicky discovered that galaxies are swarming within each cluster like bees in a hive at a much faster clip than conventional physics can explain.

NEIL DEGRASSE TYSON DARES GOVERNMENT TO 'JUST SHOW THE ALIEN,' AS DISCLOSURE FERVOR CONTINUES TO GROW

In class, I learned that these clustered galaxies would need to have roughly ten times more mass to explain their unusual swiftness. This means that most of the galaxies’ collective mass is "missing" — is invisible to us. Zwicky called this ghostly mass "dunkle materie," German for dark matter.

Scientists today offer many fanciful, high-brow explanations for dark matter, but the plain truth is that, nearly a century after Zwicky’s discovery, we still have no idea whatsoever what it is. For now, the consensus is that, like conventional matter, dunkle materie is gravitational in nature — which is why it can tug on and speed up the clustered galaxies. But, very unlike conventional matter, dunkle materie does not radiate or reflect light — which is why it’s invisible.

FROM COCKROACH MILK TO STEPPING ON SNAKES, IG NOBEL AWARDS CELEBRATES SCIENCE AT ITS ODDEST

It wasn’t the first time data from the powerful Hooker telescope near Pasadena, California, delivered a scientific bombshell. Back in 1929 American lawyer-turned-astronomer Edwin Hubble used that very same instrument to discover that the universe is expanding. Thereafter, astronomers simply assumed the expansion was slowing down, owing to the universe’s collective gravity putting the brakes on it.

But, in 1998, the story of science took yet another startling turn to the dark side, when two separate teams of astronomers discovered that the expansion of our universe is actually speeding up, not slowing down. This implies the existence of an invisible, inscrutable, repulsive "something" that permeates the whole of our universe.

At a 1998 symposium at the Australian Academy of Science in Canberra, University of Chicago cosmologist Michael Turner gave the "something" a name: dark energy. But giving the phantom material a name doesn’t explain it. To this day, as with dark matter, dark energy remains a complete mystery — notwithstanding the countless published but unsupported attempts to explain it.

The discoveries of dark matter and dark energy would rate little more than a sensational footnote in the impressive story arc of science were it not for one very inconvenient truth. Today, scientists reckon that, all told, the two shadowy spirits account for ninety-five percent of the observable cosmos (never mind the existence of the totally unobservable cosmos beyond the Cosmic Horizon). Ninety-five percent!

DR MARC SIEGEL: I WENT LOOKING FOR MIRACLES AFTER OCT. 7. I FOUND ANGELS HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

It means that what we see — even with our most powerful, most sophisticated imaging devices — is only five percent of what’s actually "out there." Which means the whole of science — all its experiments, all its theories, the entirety of what it claims to understand about our demon-haunted world — is based on a measly five percent of what’s real. The other ninety-five percent of what exists remains a complete mystery.

This, in turn, means that, far from demystifying the universe, the twisting, turning story of science is actually mystifying the universe in ways that make religion more credible, not less.

The more secrets of the macroscopic and microscopic cosmos science brings to light, the more we discover how very, very, very little we understand about reality.

The more brightly Sagan’s "candle in the dark" burns, the more it reveals the truth of the Apostle Paul’s words, stated nearly 2,000 years ago: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."

Michael Guillén, PhD, taught physics at Harvard and for fourteen years was the Emmy-winning Science Editor at ABC News. Go to www.michaelguillen.com for information about his movie, The Invisible Everywhere, and book, Believing Is Seeing.

title: ‘We feel the love’: Epstein survivors overwhelmed by messages of support at pop-up art exhibition
excerpt:
Visitors to a touring show drawing attention to Epstein’s crimes have left thousands of ‘powerful’ notes – and survivors say it means a great deal

When Danielle Bensky first went to The Donald J Trum...
body_text:
Visitors to a touring show drawing attention to Epstein’s crimes have left thousands of ‘powerful’ notes – and survivors say it means a great deal

When Danielle Bensky first went to The Donald J Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room, she didn’t know what to expect.

“What happens if I walk in and survivors’ names are just plastered everywhere?” Bensky wondered about the reading room, a traveling exhibition of Epstein investigative files, first held in a New York City gallery this May. “I was a little worried in the beginning that this would be a form of exploitation for survivors.

“Instead, it was just so beautifully done.”

The reading room is meant to bring attention to Epstein’s crimes and law enforcement’s decades-long failure to act. The former financier, who counted numerous high-profile men among his associates, was arrested in 2019 for sexual abuse of teen girls but killed himself in jail.

While Ghislaine Maxwell was arrested and found guilty of luring teen girls into Epstein’s orbit, documents reveal that law enforcement officials were well aware of their crimes decades prior. Survivors have called for greater transparency and legal actions against any other participants in their sexual abuse.

Bensky also didn’t know what would happen when David Garrett, founder of event organizer the Institute for Primary Facts, floated an idea to make the exhibit more interactive. There was a cork board in the final room and Garrett told Bensky he was going to keep it there when this exhibition opened to the public, so visitors could leave notes.

“I was like, ‘Oh, that’s such a great idea,” said Bensky, who is among the Epstein survivors pushing for accountability and justice. “That’ll be so cool to see.”

About a week after the reading room officially opened, Bensky returned and saw “at least six or seven corkboards that were full and overflowing with notes”. There were notes with drawings and notes with abject sadness and “sometimes, it was pure rage”.

“Sometimes, it would be a note directly to a survivor. Sometimes it was a note directly to themselves, and it got everybody involved,” she said. “Even members of survivors’ families were leaving notes. It was just a really beautiful display of our democracy.”

Bensky said the notes have given her hope amid years of institutional failures.

“Being seen in this process has been pretty remarkable.” Visitors have written, “We’re here with you, we stand with you, and we believe you” – demonstrating the “really beautiful empathy that comes with every single note”, Bensky said.

“There have been days where I felt like I couldn’t really do much. I felt really debilitated,” Bensky said. “The reading room can be a lot when you’re walking through your trauma all day, and you’re meeting all kinds of people.

“But so many of us will just go and sit in the room with all the notes and read the notes, and it’s like, ‘Wow, what an extraordinary thing to actually be seen and be believed by so many people at this point.’”

Liz Stein, an Epstein survivor, expressed similar sentiments about the power of these notes.

“It started out with one bulletin board, and I will never forget seeing that one initial bulletin board and just really feeling like, ‘Oh my goodness, people are really reacting to that,’” Stein said. When the first reading room installation ended, these notes “took up the better part of the downstairs of the exhibit”.

“The love that people show us is overwhelming, and every time we do these events with the reading room, every single time, people hug us, they tell us what we mean to them, and a lot of times they’ll say, ‘But it doesn’t matter. I’m just someone you don’t know from somewhere you don’t live,’” Stein said.

“And it’s like, no, we might not know your individual names, but we feel the love.”

“This wall with the note cards is a really tangible visual representation of how much support we have, and that fuels us in a way that I don’t think people quite understand.”

Garrett said that the idea for a notes space came at the last minute. He thought that people might experience deep emotions from the exhibit and might feel the need for support.

So, organizers put up a cork board with information about the national suicide prevention hotline as well as resources for those experiencing gender-based violence. Without thinking about it too much, Garrett decided to leave some extra notecards and pens.

“We just put them out and said, “if you want to write a note to the survivors, you can do that,” he told the Guardian. “We didn’t think that we would need more than that two foot by three foot corkboard.”

“By the end of the first day, not only was the corkboard full, but [notes] were taped up all around the cork board.” After just one day, visitors had left about 300 cards.

For the next 10 days, the producer would buy more cork boards everyday. There were 30 by the time the reading room ended its initial exhibition. “Every surface on that basement downstairs was full of cork boards and full of cards.”

The reading room would come to have seven stops – New York City; Washington DC; Des Moines, Iowa; Columbus, Ohio; Detroit, Michigan; Dallas, Texas; and Fort Lauderdale, Florida – and a traveling bookmobile that made about two dozen stops. In total, visitors left approximately 12,500 or 13,000 notes, Garrett said.

The reading room kicked off several months before highly contentious midterm elections dealt Republicans numerous blows which, some commentators said, was due to voters rejecting Trump. The president and Maga Republicans have been saddled by his administration’s handling of the files since he took office.

The White House rejected criticism of Trump’s handling of the files.

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

“And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House oversight committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”

Trump’s DoJ rebuffed criticism of their handling of these files and condemned the reading room.

“This sham tour is traveling to politically competitive areas and shamefully using victims as political pawns,” a DoJ spokesperson said in a statement.

“The non-profit’s fundraising ploy, which often hosts candidates for office, is a disgrace. It’s thanks to this Department of Justice that they even have those files, released in compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act under the most transparent administration to date.”

The words from supporters, both in person and notes, have provided encouragement to keep pushing for justice in spite of institutional roadblocks, Stein said.

“Your courage is louder than the people who tried to silence you,” was among Stein’s favorite notes. Another, Stein recalled, said: “One of these girls could have been me or my friends.”

“Money and power should not dictate justice,” Stein said of another memorable note.

Bensky also recalled one particularly powerful message.

“There was one that was just so simple,” Bensky recalled. “I think it literally just said: ‘It wasn’t your fault.’”

title: US datacenter demand spurs increased fossil fuel pipeline projects as rules are discarded
excerpt:
Trump administration has gutted regulations that protect lives and natural resources as pipeline build-out continues

Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when th...
body_text:
Trump administration has gutted regulations that protect lives and natural resources as pipeline build-out continues

Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.

The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

Not only has the Trump administration targeted laws that protect the environment and human health from pipelines’ risks, it has also pledged not to enforce regulations around them, the report adds.

The findings bring into focus a little-considered environmental threat in artificial intelligence and datacenter proliferation – the US already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, and these projects would almost certainly lead to more.

The pipelines could help supply the at least 98 gas-fired power plants proposed to serve datacenters, and, if all the lines are completed, they would transport about 40% more natural gas daily than what the system carries today.

“This is the largest boom in a couple decades … and it coincides with all this deregulation,” Alexandra Shaykevich, research manager with the Environmental Integrity Project, said. “That’s concerning because the pipelines do usually operate safely, but they can leak and explode, and so there are big risks for communities across the United States.”

Most of the pipelines would carry natural gas across 42 states, though many of them are concentrated in several fossil fuel-producing regions. About 42 are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana, and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois.

Advocates say they’re especially worried because of the wide-ranging attacks on foundational environmental protections, from the Clean Water Act to the Endangered Species Act, that until recently have been wielded to stop the riskiest projects, protect from accidents or hold polluters accountable.

The report states that over 25% of the projects have requested an expedited environmental review, and the administration is largely using legally dubious mechanisms to push them through, like invoking the “energy emergency”. That has accelerated permit approvals, reduced the scope of environmental studies, and limited public and community input, the report alleges.

Meanwhile, the administration has used the Defense Production Act to push through projects over the objections of states. In March, it jump-started the Santa Ynez oil pipeline in Santa Barbara, California, despite the state shutting it down in 2015 following a major spill that harmed about 150 miles (240km) of coastline. The act is also being used to attempt to ram through controversial plans for the 125-mile (200km) Constitution pipeline that would run from Pennsylvania to upstate New York, which the latter has opposed.

The Trump administration in January issued a memo stating that it would “refrain from taking any enforcement action” against companies that violated Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulations. By 2025, it had already cut the average number of enforcement actions initiated in half, recording only 117.

The administration is also raising the risk of accidents and explosions by allowing companies to increase the pressure of pipelines in densely populated areas and letting them conduct fewer pressure tests, the report alleges.

It has made changes like this despite the regularity of accidents, including some that are deadly. The report points to a March 2023 disaster in which a crack in a gas pipeline in West Reading, Pennsylvania, caused an explosion in a chocolate factory that killed seven workers and injured 10 others. Last month, two workers were killed when a New Mexico pipeline exploded.

The pipelines could also destroy thousands of acres of federally protected wetlands. At least 81 of the projects are expected to damage more than 19,000 acres (7,700 hectares) of federally protected wetlands, the report found. This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections.

The dangers of this are felt in south-west Louisiana, which holds a large concentration of pipelines because of the high number of export terminals along the Mississippi River. These already cut through and harmed sensitive wetlands and fishing grounds, said James Hiatt, executive director of For a Better Bayou.

“The people who live here carry the risks and bear the burden while the profits go elsewhere,” Hiatt said.

title: Restaurants bring back old-school hospitality as nostalgia takes hold across America
excerpt: Ford's Garage president Billy Downs discusses how the restaurant chain's automotive-themed atmosphere and connections to American history attract customers of all ages while creating memorable experie...
body_text:
Ford's Garage president Billy Downs discusses how the restaurant chain's automotive-themed atmosphere and connections to American history attract customers of all ages while creating memorable experiences for diners.

After years of modernization, restaurant chains are rediscovering the appeal of the past.

Pizza Hut has revisited its classic red-roof dining experience, while Cracker Barrel faced backlash over efforts to modernize its familiar image.

Across the industry, nostalgia has become a way to reconnect with consumers who still have an affinity for the restaurants they remember. But as chains revisit vintage decor, familiar branding and throwback menus, some restaurant operators see an opportunity to revive something less tangible: old-fashioned hospitality.

DISCONTINUED CRACKER BARREL FOODS THAT FANS ARE BEGGING TO GET BACK

At Ford's Garage, a 36-unit casual-dining chain modeled after a 1920s service station, Billy Downs has turned to an unlikely source of inspiration for the company's hospitality training program: his grandmother.

"We designed a training program that was designed after what a 'Greatest Generation' grandma would have served their family," the Michigan-based Ford's Garage president told Fox News Digital.

The hospitality program at Ford's Garage is modeled after Billy Downs' grandmother. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

The program, dubbed the "hospitality wheel," draws on the warmth and personal attention Downs remembers from visiting his grandmother, an approach the company hopes to replicate across its growing restaurant footprint.

"I'll tell you this, she made you feel special, and that's what we want people to come out of this is feel special when they go to a Ford's Garage," Downs said.

KFC UNVEILS RADICALLY DIFFERENT RESTAURANT IN MAJOR COMEBACK PUSH

That philosophy extends beyond the training program. Downs said the chain places considerable emphasis on making guests feel welcome and fostering personal connections.

"We also know that we have a unique dining experience in terms of the environment, but we want to have that hospitality be really important and we want people to get connected when they come on in," he said.

The president of Ford's Garage says hospitality and value help set the restaurant chain apart from others. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

That emphasis on personal connection comes as the restaurant industry increasingly embraces technology and automation, raising questions about the role of human interaction in the dining experience.

Chef Joe Isidori, owner of Arthur & Sons, which has locations in New York and Florida, believes that as technology becomes more prevalent, the human element of hospitality could become an increasingly valuable commodity.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

A third-generation New York City chef, Isidori told Fox News Digital that younger diners are already showing an appreciation for restaurants with authentic histories and experiences that can't easily be replicated.

"What they'll never be able to replace is the nostalgic real-life experiences," he said.

Arthur & Sons still provides a sense of nostalgia and old-school hospitality. (Arthur & Sons)

For Isidori, the stakes extend beyond nostalgia. As consumers become more selective about where they spend their dining dollars, he argues that restaurants must offer something beyond food and convenience to justify the expense of eating out.

"If they're going to spend money, it's got to have an experience to it," Isidori said.

Isidori sees a potentially bigger challenge ahead as automation advances: ensuring that restaurants don't lose the personal connections that distinguish hospitality from a purely transactional experience.

"Restaurants are really going to have a problem in 10 years," Isidori said. "I mean, the robots are coming."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

But while technology may transform how restaurants operate, Isidori believes the personal connections and memorable experiences that define hospitality will become even more valuable.

"A robot can't do what Joe Isidori does," he said. "He can't walk, talk and act like me and actually cook like me."

Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

title: Democrats’ midterm sweep opens path to bypassing Electoral College by 2028
excerpt: Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discusses criticism of the Electoral College by former 2026 Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris on ‘America R...
body_text:
Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discusses criticism of the Electoral College by former 2026 Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris on ‘America Reports.’

Democrats’ midterm gains have opened a new front in the fight over how America chooses its president — one that could reshape the 2028 race for the White House.

Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, already enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C., has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. If the four states join, their combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it. Arizona could push the total to 283 if Democrats ultimately gain control of both chambers there.

National Popular Vote (NPV), the nonprofit organization that authored the compact and is campaigning to enact it state by state, says it has identified multiple legislative sponsors in each of the five states whose combined electoral votes could push the compact over the 270-vote threshold. It expects bills to be pre-filed before, or introduced early, in the 2027 legislative sessions.

"I am confident we have multiple paths to secure the 48 electoral votes required to deliver what 63-percent of Americans want," Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant for NPV, told Fox News Digital.

VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS

A voter fills out their ballot at a polling location inside Wayne Community College - Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under the current electoral system, every state except Maine and Nebraska awards its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the statewide vote. If the compact takes effect, participating states would instead award their electors to the candidate who wins the most votes nationwide, leaving the Electoral College formally in place but making the national tally decisive.

Supporters argue the compact would give every vote equal weight by counting ballots toward a single national total. The Electoral College, by contrast, was structured to give both populous and smaller states a meaningful role in choosing the president.

"They can’t use a compact to, in essence, change the Electoral College," Hans von Spakovsky, an election law expert with the conservative group Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital when asked about the potential activation of the compact before the 2028 election.

"This is unprecedented," von Spakovsky, a former commissioner on the Federal Election Commission (FEC), continued. "In the past, the only kind of compacts that have been agreed on between states have been things like water sharing — when rivers run between states, they enter into compacts to agree on that. But a compact that changes a fundamental structural given in the Constitution, I think the Supreme Court would say you can’t do that."

HILLARY CLINTON STILL FUMING OVER ELECTORAL COLLEGE, CALLS IT AN 'ABOMINATION' IN NEW NETFLIX SERIES

A 4th grader works on an election themed art project at Heather Hills Elementary School in Bowie, Md., on Tuesday, October 22, 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Rosenstiel rejected the argument that the compact would improperly alter the Constitution, saying NPV believes Article II, Section 1 gives states the authority to determine how their presidential electors are appointed.

"Any clean read of Article II, Section 1 makes it clear that states have the exclusive power to award electors," Rosenstiel said. "The only credible legal question is whether this compact requires congressional consent."

Von Spakovsky argued that because the NPV compact is an agreement between states, Congress would have to approve it under the Constitution's Compact Clause in Article I. He noted Congress could approve the compact with simple majorities in the House and Senate and that the Constitution does not explicitly require the president’s signature — meaning a presidential veto might not stop it.

However, von Spakovsky added that states choosing not to participate in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would have a strong basis for litigation.

"Given that the NPV is entirely a creation of Democrats and only supported by Democrats, the new Congress will no doubt easily pass this compact," he told Fox News Digital. "However, I believe the non-participating states would have a good basis for litigation, which would end up in the Supreme Court, arguing that the compact is unconstitutional because it changes a fundamental structural part of the Constitution without going through the constitutional amendment process. The argument would be that states cannot make agreements among themselves that damage the federal system provided by the Constitution."

The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)

National Popular Vote’s campaign has identified sponsors in all five potential additions following the midterms that could help push the compact over its 270-vote threshold and plans to begin pushing bills before or early in the 2027 legislative sessions, according to Rosenstiel.

Rosenstiel said the compact would apply to the 2028 election only if states representing at least 270 electoral votes join before July 20 of that year. That gives state lawmakers, Congress — if approval is required — and the courts less than two years to resolve the political and constitutional questions.

Until then, the Electoral College remains unchanged.

"I’m increasingly confident we can achieve that goal and we will have a national popular vote for president in 2028. I would certainly prepare for it," he said.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discusses criticism of the Electoral College by former 2026 Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris on ‘America Reports.’

Democrats’ midterm gains have opened a new front in the fight over how America chooses its president — one that could reshape the 2028 race for the White House.

Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, already enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C., has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. If the four states join, their combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it. Arizona could push the total to 283 if Democrats ultimately gain control of both chambers there.

National Popular Vote (NPV), the nonprofit organization that authored the compact and is campaigning to enact it state by state, says it has identified multiple legislative sponsors in each of the five states whose combined electoral votes could push the compact over the 270-vote threshold. It expects bills to be pre-filed before, or introduced early, in the 2027 legislative sessions.

"I am confident we have multiple paths to secure the 48 electoral votes required to deliver what 63-percent of Americans want," Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant for NPV, told Fox News Digital.

VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS

A voter fills out their ballot at a polling location inside Wayne Community College - Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under the current electoral system, every state except Maine and Nebraska awards its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the statewide vote. If the compact takes effect, participating states would instead award their electors to the candidate who wins the most votes nationwide, leaving the Electoral College formally in place but making the national tally decisive.

Supporters argue the compact would give every vote equal weight by counting ballots toward a single national total. The Electoral College, by contrast, was structured to give both populous and smaller states a meaningful role in choosing the president.

"They can’t use a compact to, in essence, change the Electoral College," Hans von Spakovsky, an election law expert with the conservative group Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital when asked about the potential activation of the compact before the 2028 election.

"This is unprecedented," von Spakovsky, a former commissioner on the Federal Election Commission (FEC), continued. "In the past, the only kind of compacts that have been agreed on between states have been things like water sharing — when rivers run between states, they enter into compacts to agree on that. But a compact that changes a fundamental structural given in the Constitution, I think the Supreme Court would say you can’t do that."

HILLARY CLINTON STILL FUMING OVER ELECTORAL COLLEGE, CALLS IT AN 'ABOMINATION' IN NEW NETFLIX SERIES

A 4th grader works on an election themed art project at Heather Hills Elementary School in Bowie, Md., on Tuesday, October 22, 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Rosenstiel rejected the argument that the compact would improperly alter the Constitution, saying NPV believes Article II, Section 1 gives states the authority to determine how their presidential electors are appointed.

"Any clean read of Article II, Section 1 makes it clear that states have the exclusive power to award electors," Rosenstiel said. "The only credible legal question is whether this compact requires congressional consent."

Von Spakovsky argued that because the NPV compact is an agreement between states, Congress would have to approve it under the Constitution's Compact Clause in Article I. He noted Congress could approve the compact with simple majorities in the House and Senate and that the Constitution does not explicitly require the president’s signature — meaning a presidential veto might not stop it.

However, von Spakovsky added that states choosing not to participate in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would have a strong basis for litigation.

"Given that the NPV is entirely a creation of Democrats and only supported by Democrats, the new Congress will no doubt easily pass this compact," he told Fox News Digital. "However, I believe the non-participating states would have a good basis for litigation, which would end up in the Supreme Court, arguing that the compact is unconstitutional because it changes a fundamental structural part of the Constitution without going through the constitutional amendment process. The argument would be that states cannot make agreements among themselves that damage the federal system provided by the Constitution."

The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)

National Popular Vote’s campaign has identified sponsors in all five potential additions following the midterms that could help push the compact over its 270-vote threshold and plans to begin pushing bills before or early in the 2027 legislative sessions, according to Rosenstiel.

Rosenstiel said the compact would apply to the 2028 election only if states representing at least 270 electoral votes join before July 20 of that year. That gives state lawmakers, Congress — if approval is required — and the courts less than two years to resolve the political and constitutional questions.

Until then, the Electoral College remains unchanged.

"I’m increasingly confident we can achieve that goal and we will have a national popular vote for president in 2028. I would certainly prepare for it," he said.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.
