The APU-L launchers are designed to carry Russia's LMUR, a precision-guided missile also known as Product 305 or the Kh-39. The roughly 230-pound missile carries a 55-pound warhead and can be guided in flight by an operator using an electro-optical seeker and two-way radio link.

A missile is launched during an air defense drill in an undisclosed location in Iran in a handout image from Jan. 12, 2025. (Iranian Army/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE

Iran had already publicly announced plans to acquire Russian Mi-28 attack helicopters, one of the platforms capable of carrying the weapon. The first export-variant Mi-28NE helicopters were photographed in Iran in January 2026.

The paperwork also shows involvement by Russia's Defense Ministry. A May 2024 letter accompanying the K-10 production schedule was co-signed by the head of the ministry's 123rd Military Representation.

The documents do not establish whether the completed launchers ultimately reached Iran, though Dallas Analytics told Fox News Digital the contract itself is "a very strong proof" of the transfer.

SATELLITE IMAGES MAY HAVE TIPPED OFF IRAN BEFORE US BASE ATTACK, TOP REPUBLICAN WARNS

The findings add new detail to a military relationship the Trump administration has repeatedly played down during the war. U.S. intelligence has assessed that Russia provided Iran with information on the location of American military assets and, more recently, satellite imagery and weapons components, according to reports.

But administration officials have said that support has not materially affected the U.S. campaign.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russian assistance was not impeding U.S. military operations, while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said the U.S. was tracking Moscow's support and accounting for it in its battle plans.

The remains of a Russian-made, Iran-designed Shahed-136 drone, known in Russia as a Geran-2, are displayed with other recovered drones, glide bombs, missiles and rockets in Kharkiv on July 30, 2025. (Scott Peterson/Getty Images)

The Trump administration has separately sought to disrupt Iran's foreign weapons procurement as Tehran works to rebuild its military capabilities.

The Treasury Department has targeted networks it says helped Iran seek weapons and components abroad, including efforts to acquire Chinese-made man-portable air-defense systems.

Just this week, the State Department sanctioned a Russia-based individual it said was involved in efforts to help Iran procure Chinese-made man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, State Department and Department of War for comment.

title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
excerpt:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 year...
body_text:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

title: Ukraine raises Zaporizhia aid strike death toll to at least 50
excerpt:
The death toll from a Russian attack on an aid distribution centre in Ukraine’s Zaporizhia region has risen to at least 50 people, making it one of the deadliest Russian attacks this year.

Ukraine’s ...
body_text:
The death toll from a Russian attack on an aid distribution centre in Ukraine’s Zaporizhia region has risen to at least 50 people, making it one of the deadliest Russian attacks this year.

Ukraine’s emergency service announced on Friday that the toll from Monday’s strike on the village of Komyshuvakha has risen after eight more bodies were recovered from the rubble.

Acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin later said that the death toll reached 53 people, as rescuers continued their search for missing bodies for the fifth day.

Al Jazeera was not able to independently verify that figure.

Local police on Wednesday said that 59 people were listed as missing, though some might be among the bodies already found.

“As many as 39 people may still remain trapped under the debris,” they said.

As rescuers continue to work, specialists have been taking DNA samples to identify the bodies. Continuing Russian attacks have also remained a constant threat to the rescue operation.

Ukraine said that Russian aircraft bombed a former school near the front lines on Monday, which civilians used for weekly aid handouts.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a second wave of bombs then hit the underground shelter where people had taken cover, causing most of the destruction.

“After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover,” he said on X.

Four police officers and two rescue workers were also among the dead.

Zelenskyy called it a “vile terrorist strike” and said it signalled Moscow’s refusal to stop the fighting. The UN human rights mission in Ukraine also said the strike was likely a breach of international law.

The attack on Monday came only a day after a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky ended.

Russia and Ukraine both continued to trade drone attacks on Thursday, which injured several people on both sides, including a child.

On Wednesday, in the eastern Donetsk region, Russian attacks killed four civilians and injured five others.

Delegations from both Ukraine and Russia are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 for US-brokered talks, though previous rounds made little progress.

title: Russia’s land gains in Ukraine dwindle as its diesel reportedly goes unsold
excerpt:
Russia’s battlefield gains in Ukraine have fallen to almost nothing this year, according to the latest figures from independent observers and Kyiv’s military.

Territory seized by Russian forces in th...
body_text:
Russia’s battlefield gains in Ukraine have fallen to almost nothing this year, according to the latest figures from independent observers and Kyiv’s military.

Territory seized by Russian forces in the first 10 months of 2026 amounts to 117.38 sq km (45.32 sq miles), according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a Washington-based think tank that uses open-source geolocated footage.

By comparison, gains in 2025 were 5,304 sq km (2,047.95 sq miles), including 473 sq km (182.63 sq miles) of Russian territory recaptured in the Kursk region, while in 2024 they were 3,604 sq km (1,391.31 sq miles).

That means Russia advanced at a rate of 0.38 sq km (0.15 sq miles) a day this year, compared with 13.25 sq km (5.12 sq miles) a day in 2025 and 9.9 sq km (3.82 sq miles) a day in 2024.

In addition, Russia is suffering higher casualties this year.

Ukraine’s General Staff put the estimated number of Russian personnel killed or seriously wounded from January 1 to October 31 at 381,300.

Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty claims by either side.

Estimated Russian losses have repeatedly broken new monthly records for the entire war since the summer – 42,860 in July, 46,230 in September and 54,400 in October – as Ukraine’s military sought to reach a monthly target of 50,000 casualties set by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in January.

The losses are far beyond Russia’s estimated recruitment capacity of 24,000-30,000 a month.

While Russia lost firm control of Ukrainian territory in April and May, it increased its areas of infiltration, where control is contested.

In September and October, however, Russia lost both firmly controlled and infiltrated territory, ISW assessments show.

Zelenskyy and his prime minister have cited these worsening trends as the reasons why Russia is intensifying long-range strikes targeting energy infrastructure. Civilians have been killed in those attacks, leading Ukrainians to believe that Moscow is opting for psychological warfare.

Russia unleashed an unusually heavy barrage during the week ending on November 6, including 2,346 drones and more than 80 missiles across Ukraine.

The strikes reached a crescendo on November 3, with 370 drones and 76 missiles.

Hundreds of thousands of families are struggling with blackouts at the beginning of winter.

In one of Russia’s deadliest attacks this year, in the village of Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, at least 50 people were killed.

“The invaders knew that on Mondays, humanitarian aid was distributed at the Komyshuvakha resilience centre. Residents of the community come here for food, medicine, essential items,” Ukraine’s military intelligence service (GUR) said.

The attack came on the day a six-day ceasefire ended in Oleshky, 250km (155.34 miles) southwest of Komyshuvakha in the Kherson region.

Brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, the localised ceasefire was the longest ever observed and enabled the warring sides to evacuate 800 residents of the besieged town, which is in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.

Russian military reporter Vladimir Romanov was arrested by authorities in his country after reporting that Oleshky residents who had opted to go to Ukraine had filled 17 buses, while those who opted to go to Russia filled four.

Moscow has cited the alleged abuse of its Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of the main reasons for its full-scale invasion in 2022, and has claimed that it would be welcomed as a liberating force.

Ukraine resumed almost daily targeting of Russian refineries during the past week, hitting eight in seven days.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said three refineries were hit on October 30.

Ukraine hit two more refineries in the Ufa complex in the Bashkortostan Republic on October 31. The following day it struck Lukoil’s Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery in Nizhny Novgorod, and a production and dispatch station in the Samara region the day after that. It hit the Yaroslavl oil refinery on November 3, and the Ryazan oil refinery on November 5.

The strikes were designed to deprive Russia of energy and export revenue and scupper a deal reached by Russian President Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump on October 9, when the US leader invited Russia to sell 1.8 million tonnes of diesel to the global market by the end of the year to help bring down transport prices.

Trump’s invitation flew in the face of US oil sanctions and the Lindsey Graham Act the president had signed into law 11 days earlier, which gave him the power to impose sanctions on other countries buying Russian oil.

The Kremlin has since pumped four tankers full of diesel fuel, reported the Financial Times (FT), in hopes of selling it to the US and effectively ending oil sanctions against it. But those tankers have reportedly failed to find buyers willing to risk the legal consequences of purchasing Russian oil. The Kremlin dismissed the FT’s report as fake news.

On October 27, US Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-authored the Lindsey Graham Act, warned a Greek shipping company operating one of the four diesel-laden ships not to attempt to offload its cargo in the US.

“The President may have given a licence to facilitate this transaction, but only Congress can make it legally valid,” Blumenthal had written, effectively warning all shippers they would face a legal tangle between statutory law and presidential executive orders.

US courts have struck down many of Trump’s executive orders in his first two years in office.

title: Russell Brand barrister reports himself to watchdog over confrontation with journalist
excerpt:
Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward: ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’

Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself...
body_text:
Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward: ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’

Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of launching a tirade at a journalist shortly after the former comedian had been found guilty of rape.

Ian Winter KC “confronted” the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.”

Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” to which Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.”

“Congratulations,” he added, in an incident that happened outside the courtroom door at Southwark crown court on Thursday afternoon, with a group of journalists watching.

In a statement issued on Friday lunchtime, Winter said he had referred himself to the Bar Standards Board, his professional regulator.

He said: “Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today’s press, I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny.

The incident happened moments after a jury had found Brand guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault at the conclusion of a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

Brand had denied all the charges against him, and argued through his lawyer that he had been wrongly accused and was the victim of a media conspiracy.

After the trial, experts added to calls for a change in the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”.

In his closing speech, Winter said none of the complainants had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave” during their encounters with Brand.

Claire Waxman, who is the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, is seeking to update the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”. She criticised “outdated and harmful assumptions” that victims must have screamed or tried to fight off their attacker.

The head of Scotland Yard, Mark Rowley, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme he supported Waxman’s call. “I think what I’ve heard reported heads towards, it’s getting very close to victim-blaming, which is something we’ve thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don’t do.

“People fall into myths about [how] a rape victim must behave in a certain way, must react in a certain way. The evidence is really clear. Some people will fight. Some people will freeze. Some people will tell people straight away. Some people bottle it up for years. There isn’t one way of reacting.” On Friday a No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham believed that Waxman’s calls should be examined.

Speaking after the trial Urwin told a Times podcast she approached Winter after the verdict because her name had been mentioned during the trial. “I thought he’s talked about me a lot, I’ll go and introduce myself and that is a legitimate thing to do,” she said. “I was surprised to be confronted and spoken to in that way.”

It is understood that several complaints have been submitted to the Bar Standards Board but the regulator said it would not “comment as to whether or not it has received any information about potential misconduct by a barrister regardless of how any information comes to our attention”.

A spokesperson said complaints were usually handled confidentially unless they resulted in a disciplinary tribunal hearing.

The comedian Katherine Ryan criticised the barrister on her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, saying: “That was so unprofessional, so inappropriate, so aggressive. Really sickening.”

Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times, defended Urwin, his newspaper’s chief news correspondent. He said: “I found what Mr Winter did quite extraordinary. I have never seen or heard of a barrister behaving in this way. There’s a really serious point here, which is that it was not Ros who found Russell Brand guilty at Southwark crown court.

“It was a jury of eight men and four women who have sat through this case. They’ve listened to the evidence, they’ve listened to the defence, and they have gone away and they’ve come back with some very considered verdicts.

“By impugning Ros’s integrity, what Mr Winter is doing, and he should really be called to account for this, he’s impugning the integrity of the entire case.

“He’s impugning the integrity of a jury … who have sat there solemnly and done their duty, and the judge who oversaw the case and everybody else involved. I think what he did was reprehensible.”

During the trial, Winter had argued that reporting of allegations against Brand by the Times, the Sunday Times and a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary had “poisoned the well”, and rendered it impossible for his client to have a fair trial.

The trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, dismissed an attempt by Brand to block his trial from taking place because of negative media coverage.

In a pre-trial argument, Brand, through Winter, had accused the journalists who first exposed him as a sexual predator of being “criminals”, suggesting their reporting in 2023 had made a fair trial impossible and venturing that they may have committed the crime of perverting the course of justice.

But the judge rejected that attempt to stop the trial, ruling that Brand could simply be tried by people who had not seen the previous media reporting.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.

“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths but we are going further by changing the law to stop irrelevant sexual history and previous allegations being weaponised against rape victims. We will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”

Brand, 51, was convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan in 2009 and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009.

He is in custody and due to be sentenced on Monday.

title: JACKSON THOMPSON: Washington State Democratic Party calls girls' sports initiative unconstitutional
excerpt:
A Washington high school wrestler’s Supreme Court fight could help bring restrictions on transgender athletes in girls’ sports to 23 states.

Washington State Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad call...
body_text:
A Washington high school wrestler’s Supreme Court fight could help bring restrictions on transgender athletes in girls’ sports to 23 states.

Washington State Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad called a voter-approved girls’ sports measure unconstitutional and said the party would support groups seeking to challenge it in court.

"While this result is incredibly disheartening, voters in Washington and across the nation rejected anti-trans candidates up and down the ballot," Conrad said in the Nov. 5 statement. "The fight over I-638 is just beginning. We believe this initiative is unconstitutional on its face and support organizations planning to challenge it in court."

The Washington State Democratic Party sent a statement to OutKick stating, "WA Dems will not be challenging the initiative in court. We believe there will be organizations who do and we support those efforts."

WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS

The party also declined to make Conrad available for an interview.

Voters approved Initiative 638, which bars students the measure defines as biologically male from competing in girls’ K-12 athletic competitions. It also requires students seeking to compete in female-only sports to submit a health examination form or other statement from a health care provider verifying their biological sex based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels. The Associated Press called the measure as passed, with about 56.6% support in results reported by Axios.

The measure does not specify which examinations or tests providers must use. Opponents have warned it could lead to invasive exams or testing for girls. Let’s Go Washington, the group behind the initiative, says providers can rely on existing medical records and that the measure does not require genital exams. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has said its current sports physical rules do not require genital, DNA or hormone testing.

Conrad said the measure "undoes protections in Washington state law passed 20 years ago" and added, "To every trans girl participating in school sports, please know that we support your right to play." I-638 changes Washington’s longstanding policy allowing students to participate on teams consistent with their gender identity.

WASHINGTON STATE'S HIGH SCHOOL SPORTS LEAGUE PUTS ONUS FOR TRANS ATHLETE CONTROVERSY ON STATE LAWS

The statement also highlighted voters’ rejection of two other measures backed by Let’s Go Washington: I-001, concerning parental rights and access to student information, and I-645, which sought to repeal the state’s new tax on income above $1 million, which has nothing to do with girls' sports. Voters approved I-638, the third measure in the group’s 2026 ballot effort.

The Gender Justice League said it was evaluating legal options, while the ACLU of Washington declined to discuss potential litigation. I-638 is set to take effect Dec. 3, pending certification of the election results.

Conrad’s statement also pointed to Jaelynn Scott’s election to the state House. Scott is set to become Washington’s first openly transgender state legislator and the first out Black transgender woman elected to a state legislature in the country.

Here are three insert-ready paragraphs on the Washington cases:

The dispute became especially visible in Camas, where about a dozen girls on the high school cross-country team walked off before a race to protest a transgender teammate’s participation.

The runner had competed in the boys’ category earlier in the season before switching to the girls’ team; the district and the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association said her participation complied with existing rules.

Washington’s wrestling policy is also being challenged in federal court. A Puyallup student identified in court filings as K.M.K. alleges that a transgender opponent sexually assaulted her during a December 2025 girls’ match. The claim has not resulted in criminal charges.

K.M.K.’s family sued state and school officials and has asked the Supreme Court for emergency relief after lower courts denied an injunction. The Supreme Court docket showed the application remained pending as of its latest listed filing on Nov. 3.

A girls’ basketball game in Tumwater prompted a separate Title IX dispute. In February 2025, Tumwater player Frances Staudt sat out a game against Shelton after learning a transgender student was on the opposing girls’ team. A complaint filed on Staudt’s behalf alleged that the district denied her a fair opportunity to compete and retaliated against her for speaking out.

The U.S. Department of Education opened an investigation; that action was an inquiry into the allegations, not a finding that the district violated Title IX. Tumwater said it took the matter seriously and would work with the department.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: Prince, the pope, and autumn 2026: purple is hot this season
excerpt:
Spotted on Balenciaga, Celine and Valentino catwalks, purple is having a moment. If you really want to stand out, wear it with red

The colour purple has links to royalty, the Catholic church, Prince,...
body_text:
Spotted on Balenciaga, Celine and Valentino catwalks, purple is having a moment. If you really want to stand out, wear it with red

The colour purple has links to royalty, the Catholic church, Prince, Gordon Brown’s ties and Barney the dinosaur and it now has a new association – autumn 2026.

It has been deemed fashion’s favourite colour having been spotted on autumn/winter catwalks, with Balenciaga, Celine and Valentino showcasing all-purple designs.

Jennifer Lawrence and Zoë Kravitz have also been spotted wearing purple, while Naomi Ackie and Nicola Peltz have worn it on the red carpet. The high street is in on the trend too, with Cos, H&M and Asos selling purple knitwear and accessories.

This season’s shade has been called “royal purple” – a vivid take on the colour, rather than a darker plum or muted lilac. This is a contrast to the neutrals that have dominated fashion in recent years.

In fact, fashion insiders are leaning into the bright theme by often pairing purple with red. Vogue recently declared that autumn’s “coolest colour clash” had arrived.

In 2024, the trend forecasting agency WGSN predicted that the colour – a shade it called “fresh purple” – would be fashionable this autumn. Sara Maggioni, WGSN’s head of womenswear, sees its popularity as part of a wider shift. “[We are seeing] a growing appetite for brighter, more expressive shades,” she says. “This reflects a gradual move away from the restraint of quiet luxury as consumers become more confident in using colour to express their personal style.”

Purple is sometimes seen as a “tricky” colour by designers because it’s hard to ignore. This now may be part of its selling point. “A couple of months ago I loathed it,” says Daisy Murray, the fashion commerce editor at Grazia. “It was a lightbulb moment for me – I’m a big fan of a bold red, particularly in summer, so a punchy purple suddenly made sense.”

Kassia St Clair, the author of The Secret Lives of Colour, says purple has long been linked to the wealthy and powerful. Tyrian purple is associated with the Romans – when dye was made from the secretions of molluscs near the ancient city of Tyre. However, with the mollusc population declining and the collapse of the Byzantine empire in 1453, the method for making the dye was lost. “But the reputation of purple lingers,” St Clair says.

The problem was solved in 1856 when the chemist William Henry Perkin accidentally created a bright purple liquid while attempting to find a treatment for malaria. The first chemical dye, which Perkin called mauve, began to be produced, and Queen Victoria and her granddaughter Princess Eugenie began to wear it. St Clair says purple became so popular that the satirical magazine Punch said everyone in London had “caught the mauve measles”.

Purple’s associations with the elite remain today. “We do still have a simmering cultural awareness of the associations between purple and power,” says St Clair. “These things persist for an extraordinarily long time despite the fact people don’t know the history.”

Maggioni argues that purple’s popularity is bolstered by a more modern context, too. “[Fresh purple] has a ‘phygital’ quality – it can work across physical settings and virtual worlds,” she says. “Its vivid, slightly otherworldly character suits digital imagery and immersive environments, where colour can be intensified [and] transformed.”

Of course, purple clothing is worn in the real world – with something as prosaic as the weather a factor. “[Red and purple are the] colours of autumn and winter – think heather and rosehips,” says Murray. “There’s something about purple that really suits dark evenings,” adds St Clair. “It’s hard to imagine it in beautiful spring light.”

title: Valencia vs Real Madrid: La Liga – preview, team news, predictions
excerpt:
Who: Valencia vs Real Madrid
What: La Liga
Where: Mestalla Stadium, Valencia, Spain
When: Saturday, November 7, at 9pm (20:00 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from...
body_text:
Who: Valencia vs Real Madrid
What: La Liga
Where: Mestalla Stadium, Valencia, Spain
When: Saturday, November 7, at 9pm (20:00 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 17:00 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream

Jose Mourinho’s Madrid visit Valencia knowing that a win will provisionally draw them level with league leaders Barcelona.

Madrid have had some wobbles so far this season, but have won their last seven games in all competitions – including four in the league and an El Clasico win over Barca since a 2-1 defeat to Atletico Madrid in September.

Mourinho’s side are currently third in the La Liga table, three points behind the leaders Barcelona, with the Catalan side set to play second placed Atletico on Sunday.

Valencia will be hoping to inject some life into their season as they go into the weekend second bottom of the table, having taken just nine points from 11 games.

Madrid’s coach lavished praise on Jude Bellingham after the midfielder scored a brilliant back-heeled goal against AEK Athens in the Champions League on Wednesday.

On a night when Bellingham became the youngest player to make 60 appearances in European club football’s top competition, the England midfielder scored and was named player of the match as Madrid rallied to a 3-2 win.

“He is a unique player. Today, there is no midfielder in world football like Jude, who is complete on all levels,” Mourinho said.

“I don’t have many words because, for me, he is an absolutely extraordinary player. Even on a day when he doesn’t have a great match, one of those jaw-dropping performances, he still brings work, leadership, ambition, quality, and goal-scoring ability. He is an extraordinary player.”

Bellingham, who was also the youngest player to make 50 appearances, reached his latest landmark at the age of 23 years, 128 days, overtaking iconic former Madrid goalkeeper Iker Casillas.

He struck in the 32nd minute by connecting with Marc Cucurella’s cross and flicking a first-time shot past goalkeeper Alberto Brignoli.

“It was just instinct really,” he said. “I found myself in a good position and managed to do the only thing that came naturally in that position. It was a nice one.”

Coach Javier Aguirre said his Valencia side needed the win over Elche last weekend, which came courtesy of a second half goal by substitute Nigerian striker Sadik.

“It’s a very important win for us, because we’d come off three matches without a victory, and now we have Real Madrid CF coming up. We couldn’t afford to get cut adrift,” he said.

“Getafe CF and RCD Espanyol both won, so if we hadn’t done likewise, a rather large gap would have opened up.”

“It’s a very significant win, both in terms of the result and the performance.”

Mourinho, Real Madrid: “This match is one of the toughest matches in the entire Spanish league. Valencia’s coach is extremely difficult, he has great experience, he knows what he wants, and he has a clear philosophy in working with teams, so it will be a very difficult match.”

Aguirre, Valencia: “You don’t need extra motivation for that game. We’ll be playing against one of the best sides in the world, and I hope that we have a good game.”

title: How Paraguay’s Ueno collapse is only its latest banking crisis
excerpt:
Paraguay’s president impeached amid bank collapse crisis

Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital bank, which has plunged the Sout...
body_text:
Paraguay’s president impeached amid bank collapse crisis

Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital bank, which has plunged the South American country into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade.

Pena announced his resignation on Thursday, but politicians formally filed impeachment charges against the president. Pena, a former International Monetary Fund (IMF) economist, then requested a 72-hour extension to present his defence at an impeachment hearing, because he had been given less than 12 hours to answer “an accusatory writ and about 300 pages of attachments”, adding: “That is not due process.”

However, the Senate convened a rare session on Friday to consider Pena’s political future, opting to move forward with efforts to remove him from office.

Until March 2025, Pena held a stake in Grupo Vazquez, the parent company that owns Ueno Bank.

Ueno Bank was established in 1976 and remained a small financial operation for decades.

After being granted a full banking licence in 2023, it rebranded and grew to become a household name in Paraguay within five years. Customers were incentivised with cashback offers on groceries and it built a network of more than 70 branches. The bank sponsored Paraguay’s national football team and its name was plastered across the country’s main stadium.

Ueno bank reported that it had 3 million customers, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adult population.

The digital bank managed $800m of public funds, including about $380m invested by Paraguay’s state pension and health fund, according to data from the Central Bank of Paraguay.

On Monday, Paraguay’s central bank decided to put Ueno bank into resolution – the strongest action it can take short of placing the bank into liquidation – after finding that its solvency ratio, a measure of its capital against its risk-weighted assets, had dropped to less than half of the legal requirement.

Resolution allows regulators to transfer a failing bank’s deposits to other institutions before liquidating remaining assets.

Customer accounts were frozen, leaving millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their savings and unpaid wages.

Ueno Bank’s nearly 3 million customers still cannot withdraw cash, make digital payments or use their bank cards.

“Santiago Pena and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder,” he added, an apparent reference to the right-wing Colorado Party which has ruled Paraguay almost uninterrupted for more than seven decades.

Regulators at Paraguay’s central bank found a pattern of risky lending to “insiders”, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. This means that executives or major investors of a bank have approved questionable, low-security loans for themselves, their families or their own businesses. In this case, Ueno had loaned $146m to companies tied to its owner, Grupo Vasquez, which has links to Paraguay’s president.

Investigators found loaned amounts went beyond legal limits and were not backed up by enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.

Central Bank regulators found Ueno’s loans to companies linked to its owners were poorly documented while the bank had wrongly counted some expenses as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, was revealed to be less than half the legal minimum.

Protesters blame President Pena personally for the crisis because of his ties to the failed bank. Until recently, he held a financial stake in Ueno Bank’s parent holding company. After taking office in 2023, Pena appointed the former head of Ueno’s predecessor company, Carlos Carvallo, to head the country’s central bank, giving an insider the role of overseeing the institution. Carvallo has resigned from his position.

Pena denies any improper ties to the bank.

Protesters also say they are unhappy that so much public pension money was invested with the bank under Pena despite warnings about its high-risk insider lending practices.

Paraguay’s Congress rushed through a law on Wednesday, providing a state-guaranteed fund for repaying depositors within five business days, starting on Thursday with small accounts holding up to $1,600.

The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97 percent of customers.

Paraguay’s Public Prosector’s office has ordered multiple criminal investigations. On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, to be detained pending trial, while two others were placed under house arrest. In all, prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud.

Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena has tried to step down and wants Congress to approve his resignation. However, opposition politicians want him to be formally removed from office rather than merely allowing him to resign. They argue that allowing Pena to step down would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life and shield him from possible prosecution.

Paraguay’s Attorney General Emiliano Rolon Fernandez has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Pena and other current and former government officials, the prosecutor’s office said on Thursday.

The investigations will examine authorities’ oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender.

No. Paraguay has a long history of bank failures and went through a prolonged banking crisis from the mid-1990s to the early 2000s.

In 1995, the central bank was forced to close Bancopar, which had severe liquidity problems and had also practised insider lending to companies linked to the bank’s owners. Three more banks also failed because of risky practices and poor oversight. The government was forced to cover the deposits of customers of all four banks, causing lasting damage to public confidence in Paraguay’s banking system.

Other banks including Banco General, and Banco Aleman were closed in this era. Banco Union and the state-linked Banco Nacional de Trabajadores and Banco Plus also failed.

Banco Espirito Santo in Portugal collapsed in 2014 with losses of $4.8bn when it was revealed that the family-controlled banking group had hidden losses. The Bank of Portugal had to split and rescue what was the country’s second largest private bank. That happened as Portugal was recovering from a deep recession, austerity cuts and bail-out obligations to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the European Central Bank (ECB) and the European Commission.

In 2008, the three major commercial banks in Iceland – Glitnir, Kaupthing and Landsbanki – all collapsed within days following the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers. The three banks were heavily exposed because they had borrowed from foreign capital markets far too aggressively. Iceland did not shore up the banks, instead seeking help from the IMF and launching criminal investigations.

The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered banking crises in other countries, including the United Kingdom, but banks there were mostly propped up or rescued by governments.

Fraud and insider lending caused the collapse of Banco Intercontinental Baninter in the Dominican Republic in 2003 with losses of $2.2bn.

And in 1991, Bank of Credit and Commerce International, a globally active bank, collapsed with losses of $10bn. Extensive fraud, hidden bad loans, and illicit operations masked the true scale of the deficit until the intervention of regulators. It was shut it down simultaneously in more than 70 countries.

title: Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, arrested in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material
excerpt:
Father of the Duchess of Sussex was taken into custody near Tampa, US prosecutors said

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on Frid...
body_text:
Father of the Duchess of Sussex was taken into custody near Tampa, US prosecutors said

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on Friday and charged in connection with possession of child sexual abuse material, according to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

Markle, 82, was taken into custody at a nursing home near Tampa early on Friday, and was expected to appear in court in Tampa in the early afternoon, the US justice department said in a statement.

A 14-page federal criminal complaint says that agents seized approximately 78 items and alleges that Markle kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units that he rented for nearly two decades. An affidavit filed with the ​complaint that led to the arrest stated that two of the images inside the units showed a man identified by a witness as Markle with a nude underage girl.

The document, filed in federal court in California, said the recovered material included dozens of slides, photographs, film negatives and books containing the illegal material. It said the FBI was still reviewing the material.

The director of the FBI, Kash ​Patel, said: “Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his ⁠criminal actions. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero ⁠safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”

Some details on the criminal complaint are redacted, such as the name of the federal agent who signed the complaint, who states that they are assigned to the violent crimes against children unit in the LA office of the FBI. The case is presented as United States of America v Thomas Wayne Markle.

“Mr Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the central district of California, said in a statement.

“These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

Markle is charged with one count of possession of child sexual abuse material, and faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.

Meghan, the wife of Prince Harry, said last month that she was “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images was found at her father’s former home in the Philippines.

The duchess also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about her father was sent to police in London in 2018.

She had issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his Philippines residence. He was named as a person of interest in the case earlier this week.

According to the justice department statement, FBI agents interviewed a person last month who was aware that Markle was renting the two storage units in California after the bureau became aware of developments in the Philippines.

Markle rented the units since 2008, it said, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Photographs produced by the Daily Mail showed Thomas Markle Sr being taken away in a wheelchair, in handcuffs, wearing a black T-shirt and surrounded by agents wearing jackets marked “FBI”. The UK tabloid asked Markle if he was a pedophile and he replied: “No.” Markle did not answer when the newspaper asked if he had ever collected child sexual abuse material.

A spokesperson for the duchess did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Authorities in the Philippines, where Markle ⁠had previously lived for some time, began investigating him last month over allegations he ​possessed child sexual abuse ​images. British police last month said they ​would refer allegations about him to overseas law enforcement agencies after finding that ​claims had not ‌been passed to ​other authorities when ​they were first received.

He has denied the accusations, telling the Daily Mail they were untrue and “sick lies”.

Markle is a retired television lighting and photography director and he did not attend the wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan, amid acrimony and estrangement between father and daughter. Meghan has since said she decided to distance herself from him to protect her children.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

title: Trump will be blocked from putting ‘rightwinger’ on supreme court, Schumer says
excerpt:
After midterm wins, Democratics plan comeback for when new Congress is sworn in, including pushback against Trump and his policies

Donald Trump will be blocked from putting a “rightwinger” on the US ...
body_text:
After midterm wins, Democratics plan comeback for when new Congress is sworn in, including pushback against Trump and his policies

Donald Trump will be blocked from putting a “rightwinger” on the US supreme court, according to Chuck Schumer, the soon-to-be Senate majority leader, in remarks that were a preview of how Democrats intend to wield their power come January.

In an interview with the Associated Press, Schumer said Democrats would not confirm “any crappy nominees” to the supreme court, lower courts or Trump’s cabinet.

“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a rightwinger on the court,” Schumer said. Four supreme court justices are in their 70s, and its two most conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, are the oldest on the court at 78 and 76 years old, respectively.

After scoring massive midterm-election wins and taking back both chambers of Congress, Democratic leaders are planning their comeback for when the new Congress is sworn in. That includes major pushback against the US president and his policies.

Some Democrats are planning to launch investigations into Trump and members of his administration. On Tuesday evening, Robert Garcia, the soon-to-be chair of the House oversight committee, warned Republicans to “lawyer up”.

Others are preparing to push forward legislation they promised to voters, and Democratic leaders will enjoy wide margins in both the House and Senate to pass key priorities like restoring Medicaid cuts from Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and halting funding for the war in Iran. Trump has indicated he plans to veto bills he doesn’t agree with.

Democrats have secured 54 Senate seats for the next Congress, and that number would increase to 56 if Democratic candidates in Mississippi and Alaska triumph. Neither race has been called, but the Democrats lead in both. Democrats also will have at least 253 House seats after flipping more than 40 seats, as of Friday morning.

Schumer told the Associated Press he anticipates Democrats will have enough power to reject Trump’s nominees and halt other policies.

The supreme court is one area where Democrats plan to push back heavily.

During his first term, Trump nominated three justices to the supreme court, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, which solidified a 6-3 conservative majority that has batted away many – though not all – of the challenges to Trump’s second term policies.

Thomas or Alito still have six weeks left of a Republican Senate that could in theory confirm a Trump appointee to the high court, but Thomashas not indicated he plans to retire.

Alito denied rumors he was retiring and reiterated his plan to Fox News on Thursday, telling the news organization he plans to stay on the court for the remainder of the term, regardless of Democrats’ sweeping win.

As Democrats prepare for their return, Republicans are reflecting on how and why they lost so badly.

Over the last few days, top Republicans have played the blame game, pointing fingers at Trump’s war with Iran and tariffs for raising everyday costs.

JD Vance, the vice-president, acknowledged how the Iran war caused widespread frustrations. Ted Cruz, a senator from Texas, said Trump’s tariffs drove up costs. Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida, admitted Republicans’ vote on the Epstein files reflected poorly on the party.

Trump, meanwhile, has directed his attention to personal issues – largely related to construction projects in Washington DC.

But he suffered another blow on Friday when a federal judge blocked construction work from beginning on his planned triumphal arch for 14 days, after it was given the go ahead on Thursday by a commission packed with Trump loyalists.

On Monday, the day before the consequential elections, the US president held a press conference to unveil his administration’s latest upgrades to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The costly and controversial project has been in and out of headlines over the last year because administration officials sought to blame “vandals” for the project’s failures. A Trump-appointed US attorney later determined those failures were the result of poor work.

On Wednesday, the day after Republicans lost the majority in Congress, Trump held another press conference to show off the latest renovation to the White House ballroom, another costly and controversial project.

The US president spent more than 20 minutes discussing the details of his ballroom and only addressed his party’s massive failures when reporters asked him directly about it.

On Thursday, after suffering even more losses in Congress, Trump held a press conference in the Oval Office to sign a proclamation preventing future presidents from changing the design of his gilded Oval Office and Cabinet Room.

“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” Trump said on Thursday.

title: Nick Saban speaks truth on CFP expansion: ‘There’s not 24 teams’ that can win a national title, but money wins
excerpt:
"There are no dominant teams in college football. There's no juggernaut out there. Like this time a year ago, you really could tell Indiana was legitimate, that they were a powerhouse."

The impending...
body_text:
"There are no dominant teams in college football. There's no juggernaut out there. Like this time a year ago, you really could tell Indiana was legitimate, that they were a powerhouse."

The impending expansion of the college football playoff has led to fans sounding off on the decision to move from 12 to 24 teams after only three years after adding eight teams to the current format.

There have certainly been questions as to why it was so important from a timing standpoint to make the drastic move in adding 12 teams in such a short period of time, as ESPN and the CFP finalize their new television rights agreement over the next few weeks.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

While most of it has centered around the need to give more college football teams the opportunity at competing for a national championship, and providing conferences with justification for their spending to be competitive, a majority of fans have made it clear that making this type of leap is not worth the hassle that comes with it.

But, the most obvious argument comes down to the fact that there are not 24 teams in college football worthy enough of winning a national championship, especially in this era of the sport with teams spending upwards of $45 million to piece together a roster.

The real reason is somewhere in the middle between justifying that amount of money spent on contending for a title and what each school is doing to compete on a yearly basis with no guaranteed return on investment.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S MEGA ROSTERS AREN’T DELIVERING A RETURN ON INVESTMENT AS LSU, TEXAS A&M AND OREGON PROVE

"Too many. There’s not 24 teams in the country that can win a National Championship," Nick Saban told the Kelce brothers on the New Heights podcast. "So, what is the reason to actually do it? It’s about the money. What you’re giving up, which I hate to see, the SEC Championship Game, playing in the SEC Championship was a big thing for our players, it was a big thing to our fans. It was a tradition and it was a great venue.

"I mean, there’s only two teams who can play in a National Championship, but more teams can play in those kind of championship games. There’s a lot of pride in winning the conference championship."

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANDING TO 24 TEAMS IN 2027, WITH MORE GAMES COMING TO CAMPUSES ACROSS THE COUNTRY

ESPN College GameDay analyst Nick Saban talks during the show on the lawn of Ayres Hall at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville, Tenn., on Sept. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)

Losing out on conference title games, which is coming, was one of the caveats that committee members seemingly had to agree on in this impending move.

Now, even if some years they are meaningless when it comes to CFP rankings, the tradition that comes with the first weekend of December is lost with expanding once again.

Saban made a point that playing teams like Florida or Georgia while both ranked within the Top-5 of the country at the time added to the intrigue.

Nick Saban, former head football coach at the University of Alabama, arrives for testimony before the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation in the Hart Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C., on June 3, 2026. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

But, it was the former Alabama coach that made one of the strongest points of the entire argument, and it centers around how many games college football players will now be asked to play on a yearly basis if they are lucky enough to make a playoff run.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANDING AGAIN, BUT THE MONEY BEHIND IT IS NOT WHAT SOME WOULD CALL A 'WIN'

"We’re gonna give that up to have an extra game where the 24th team is going to play the ninth best team," Nick Saban continued. "If we just put the right 12 teams in and didn’t go through all the political BS that we went through so we can have a 12-team Playoff, and end up putting a couple of teams in that shouldn’t be in, and some teams that should’ve been in that didn’t get in should have gotten in, that was a good tournament.

"Maybe you go to sixteen if you want to include some other people. But, 24 is a lot. It's too many games for college football players to play. We played 15 games three times, and I thought that was too many games for college players to play."

Alabama Crimson Tide head coach Nick Saban looks on before the SEC Championship game against the Georgia Bulldogs at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Dec. 2, 2023. (John David Mercer/USA TODAY Sports)

Saban has a solid point, especially when those teams who compete in a conference title game then will not play another game for nearly a month.

We might not agree with the former Alabama coach on a lot of things, but Saban speaking truth into the downside of expansion is something a lot of fans will rightfully get behind.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
excerpt:
Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues

A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affect...
body_text:
Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues

A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.

The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK.

Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport’s management said it was operating normally.

The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

A number of European media outlets – including news organisations in Bulgaria, Ireland and the UK – have reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats sent an email to several outlets warning of further attacks on transport across Europe.

“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said.

The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France, two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.

A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.

“It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society,” said Martin, adding that European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.

The British broadcaster ⁠Sky said on Friday it had also received a ⁠security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.

Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it was unclear whether the hoaxes and recent cyber-attacks were “all connected”.

She added: “But they definitely all tell us the same thing: today, what is under attack are civilian infrastructures.”

The Nato alliance continued to monitor the situation and was working closely with allies, according to a senior Nato military official.

Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries were continuing.

Several European media outlets in Bulgaria, Ireland, the UK and elsewhere reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats warned in an email of further actions against transport across Europe.

“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said. The Guardian has chosen not to reproduce the email in full, given its unsubstantiated claims.

Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016. In a Telegram post on Friday the group’s founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied involvement and said the group had not existed since 2021.

Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern.

“It ⁠cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.

“The ​most reasonable assumption is that we are facing ​an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form ​of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.

Mark Rowley, the chief of London’s Metropolitan police, urged a measured response, saying past experience with the paramilitary Irish Republican Army offered valuable lessons.

He recalled the phrase “10p terrorism”, when a hoax bomb call made from a coin-operated phone box could disrupt an entire city, forcing authorities to distinguish between genuine and false threats.

The authorities would need to adapt to an evolving threat landscape involving actors around the world, some backed by hostile states, he said.

“We are going to have to adapt to that same methodology to make sure that we don’t overreact to every message we get online,” he told BBC Radio 4.

title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
excerpt:
Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children

A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all bu...
body_text:
Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children

A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Alongside 27 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.

Ahead of sentencing, prosecutors in the court in Mombasa had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie because of the gravity of the crimes.

The prosecutors also cited what they described as Mackenzie's lack of remorse for the crimes. They requested life sentences for his co-accused.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives in Shakahola forest, including two grandchildren, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".

Mackenzie and the co-accused have formally pleaded for mercy and asked for leniency from the court.

Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.

Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Diana Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.

Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.

One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".

Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.

The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.

Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.

The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.

More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest

The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.

The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.

"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen", says Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.

Wanje says a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.

"It was his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."

The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.

Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.

The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.
