title: K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report
excerpt:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors

The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waive...
body_text:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors

The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”.

A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17.

The contracts banned the performers from having an “insincere attitude” and engaging in “inappropriate romantic relationships”. They also struck standard child protection language which protected “basic human rights” including the group members’ right to education.

The contracts from record label Ador (a subsidiary of Hybe, home of popular groups BTS and Katseye) additionally excluded portions of the Korean government’s K-pop contract template stipulating that the label “shall not demand that a performer who is a minor engage in excessive physical exposure or overly sexually suggestive expression”.

In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe representatives said the company adheres to child-protection laws and works hard to make sure its artists work and train in safe conditions.

NewJeans are one of the decade’s most popular K-pop acts. In 2023, the five-member group followed Blackpink to become the second Korean girl-group to score a number one album on the Billboard charts. In November 2024, the band made global headlines when they announced their decision to leave the label amid contract disputes and claims that Ador had deliberately undermined their careers.

Band member Hanni alleged that NewJeans were mistreated by the label and accused Ador of “deliberate miscommunications and manipulation” in a statement to South Korea’s parliament last year.

Ador has consistently maintained that they did not violate their duty. “A unilateral claim that trust has been broken does not constitute valid grounds for termination of a contract,” the label said in a statement.

The label sued band member Danielle, a member of her family and the band’s producer in December 2025 for a total of nearly $30m for damages and a contract break penalty.

Hybe representatives told the New York Times that its exit penalty fees do not exceed industry standards.

In July, the group promised that 2026 would be the “summer of NewJeans,” with a teaser showing the group as a four-piece sans Danielle. New music has yet to emerge.

The new reports expose the shadowy world of K-pop contracts and shine a light on the restrictive conditions that the genre’s biggest stars can be subject to.

By the time they signed their contracts, the NewJeans members – Minji, Hanni, Haerin, Hyein and Danielle – had already clocked in years of training in K-pop “boot camps” which taught vocal training, choreography and foreign language education.

Schedules were strict, one source told the New York Times, and it was not unusual for rehearsals to stretch as late as 2am. NewJeans’s youngest member, Hyein, was 12 at the time.

After the band members received their exclusive contracts with Ador in January 2022, the parents of one member requested multiple changes. They were told that the “contract itself” could be reconsidered if it was not signed in its current form.

In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe said its contracts were legal and negotiated in good faith, with protections in place for the artist as well as the label’s investment in them.

That contract also struck government language that forbade performers working for “excessive periods of time”. It also stipulated that the band would have to repay a significant percentage of the plastic surgery costs that are common in K-pop.

“We do not even recommend cosmetic surgery or procedures against an individual’s wishes,” Hybe said in a statement.

The NewJeans contact also granted Ador rights to use the band members’ “name, photographs, likeness, handwriting, voice and any other elements” in perpetuity, in a level of ownership that goes further than government recommendations for such rights to end at the point of contract termination.

The clause also grants Ador the right to use the NewJeans members as AI chatbots or clones.

The Guardian has reached out to Hybe for comment.

title: Paraguay President Pena resigns in wake of bank collapse
excerpt: Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned on Thursday after calls for his removal swelled following the collapse of digital lender ueno that left millions of customers unable ‌to access their accoun...
body_text:
Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned on Thursday after calls for his removal swelled following the collapse of digital lender ueno that left millions of customers unable ‌to access their accounts.

“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” he said in a video recorded address on Thursday.

Pena, an ally of US President Donald Trump, is stepping down after the ⁠opposition called an extraordinary session to begin the process of filing an impeachment motion in Congress, and as protesters demanded his resignation.

Earlier on Thursday Pena lost backing from members of his own conservative party. Vice President Pedro Alliana is set to take office as his replacement.

Lawmakers had accused Pena of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to the collapse of ueno, which had grown ‌quickly ⁠from a niche fintech player into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850 million in public funds.

“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.

“The congress right now is tying to impeach the president and the vice president, this session is underway,” she added. “As a I speak, there are people outside urging congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”

Paraguay’s central bank intervened in ueno after determining ⁠that it had breached minimum solvency requirements, setting off a crisis that has left the company’s roughly 3 million customers, in a ⁠country of 6.5 million people, unable to access accounts.

“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfill its purpose, and that ⁠public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.

Ueno has made no public statement on the issue.

title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
excerpt:
Judge says actor and comedian faces ‘significant custodial term’ after being convicted of raping a woman and assaulting three others

Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually a...
body_text:
Judge says actor and comedian faces ‘significant custodial term’ after being convicted of raping a woman and assaulting three others

Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women, ending a years-long legal saga that has raised questions about how he was able to commit his crimes at the height of his fame.

Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was accused of raping women in a hotel room, in a bar toilet and at his luxury London townhouse. He sexually assaulted women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, at a radio station and TV studio.

The Hollywood actor turned online influencer was accused of gaslighting his victims after the attacks, and treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.

It can now be revealed that Brand is under investigation for two further rape allegations and that the Metropolitan police have submitted files to the Crown Prosecution Service.

On Thursday, Brand stood outside the door of the dock shortly before the jury delivered their verdicts and looked at his wife, Laura, saying: “Laura, I love you.”

Wearing a grey three-piece suit, he appeared to be praying in the dock before he was convicted of four offences on Thursday after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court.

He had pleaded not guilty to three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999.

Brand had claimed he could not remember some of the incidents, and that others had been consensual sexual encounters that had been “reimagined” or “unfavourably reframed” after the publication of sexual misconduct allegations against him in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, and Times and Sunday Times reports.

Brand closed his eyes as a jury found him guilty of four offences against four women after eight hours and 30 minutes of deliberations. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, praised the panel of four women and eight men, and told Brand: “You’ve been convicted of a number of offences, including one of rape. The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I have to therefore remand you in custody.”

Brand held his head high and appeared emotionless as he was led away by the dock officers down to the cells. His wife appeared visibly upset and left the court soon after.

His barrister, Ian Winter KC, made a plea for Brand to be given bail over the weekend as an “act of humanity” so that he could say goodbye to his children, but the judge refused.

Bennathan said he regretted the “hardship” caused to the children but said: “Whatever the good intentions of the family and the defendant today, I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence.”

As the judge remanded him into custody, Brand made “OK” gestures and said “I’m good, I’m good, I’m good”, before being taken out of the dock.

On Thursday the Met said its investigation into Brand was continuing.

Brand was found guilty of anally raping a young fan at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd after one of his gigs at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.

She told the court she begged him to stop but Brand continued. “I felt like I couldn’t speak or breathe, the amount of pain,” she said.

He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman who worked for MTV by grabbing her breasts at a birthday party in Soho, London in 2004. But he was cleared of orally raping the woman in a toilet afterwards.

He was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman who told the court that Brand laughed after squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at the radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005.

Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker, who said she was “repulsed” when Brand placed his head in her lap so she could feel his breath on her “vagina” during a filming project in 2009.

He was cleared of raping a woman after the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999, and also found not guilty of attempting to indecently assault an MTV worker by trying to drag her into a men’s toilets in 2001.

Brand’s trial heard victims had been haunted by their encounters with the former presenter and that they had bravely come forward to the tell the truth after realising they were not alone.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said they described a similar pattern of behaviour from the comedian that started with compliments, flattery and flirting before a “personality change”. “His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty,” she said.

But Brand’s barrister denied the TV personality was a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal”.

The barrister also said that the 2023 media reports had “poisoned the well” of justice, and rendered it impossible for Brand to have a fair trial.

Outside the courtroom there was an extraordinary exchange between Winter and the Sunday Times journalist who was involved in the 2023 investigation, Rosamund Urwin.

He said to her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself”. After she replied: “I’m pleased justice has been done”, Winter said: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.” He then added: “Congratulations.”

Brand’s case has led to difficult questions for the BBC, Channel 4 and the production companies that worked with him. The TV world is again asking itself whether recent efforts to improve safeguarding will stop similar abuses.

In a statement on Thursday, Channel 4 said: “We recognise the profound impact of these crimes and commend the extraordinary courage of all those who gave evidence as prosecution witnesses at trial.”

A BBC spokesperson said that a 2025 report had examined how complaints about Brand’s conduct were handled, looking at eight allegations from his time at the BBC, and added: “It was of great concern to us that some people felt unable to raise concerns about Brand’s behaviour. We apologised to those impacted, for both the culture and failings at the time, and we reiterate that apology again today.”

title: Washington state passes ballot measure banning trans girls from school sports
excerpt:
Measure in blue state requires female athletes prove their sex, which critics warn could lead to ‘invasive’ genital exams

Voters in Washington state have passed a ballot measure banning transgender g...
body_text:
Measure in blue state requires female athletes prove their sex, which critics warn could lead to ‘invasive’ genital exams

Voters in Washington state have passed a ballot measure banning transgender girls from playing on girls’ sports teams, a major loss for LGBTQ+ rights in a solidly Democratic state.

The measure says students in elementary, middle and high school who want to join girls’ athletics must first submit statements from their healthcare providers verifying their “biological sex”. Opponents have raised alarms the measure may force girls to endure “invasive and extreme” genital exams to participate in school sports.

Initiative 638 passed with support from nearly 57% of voters as of Thursday morning, though votes were still being counted.

More than 25 states across the US have adopted similar bans on trans youth athletes, mostly through legislation pushed by Republican lawmakers. Voters in Arizona and Nebraska approved similar ballot measures this week, and a ban proposed in Colorado was leading in early results, but that race has not yet been called.

Prohibiting trans youth from sports has become a major priority of conservatives and anti-LGBTQ+ groups who argue that they are protecting “fairness” in women’s athletics. But civil rights advocates say the policies are discriminatory and unnecessary, noting that trans youth have long played sports and that the restrictions target a small group of students already facing extreme prejudice and exclusion.

The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association said earlier this year that it was aware of only about 10 trans middle and high school sports players, a tiny fraction of the more than 200,000 students competing statewide. The state has for nearly two decades allowed trans students to play on teams that match their gender identity.

Critics of the sports bans argue they subject all girls to harmful scrutiny of their bodies, with opponents of Initiative 638 warning it could “force tens of thousands of Washington girls each year to undergo invasive, embarrassing, and potentially harmful genital exams just to play sports”.

More than 140 healthcare providers issued a statement opposing Washington’s measure, with Kelsey Gellner, a Seattle-based pediatric nurse, saying last month: “I tell my kids and patients that my No 1 job is to keep them safe. I can say with confidence that girls do not want to have an unnecessary exam that creates an unsafe barrier.”

The initiative was introduced in 2025 by a political action committee called Let’s Go Washington, which was founded by Brian Heywood, a hedge fund manager who has funded conservative measures. The measure was considered the most restrictive of the four trans youth sports bans on state ballots this year, as it mandates that girls prove their sex through hormone or genetic tests, or genital examinations. The measure only applies to women’s sports, and boys are not required to undergo any similar procedures.

Medical professionals have also criticized the measure for not allowing doctors to rely on birth certificates to confirm a patient’s eligibility to play on girls’ sports teams, with Libby Loft, a family physician in Spokane, saying: “I have to examine someone’s reproductive anatomy – that seems inappropriate to me for a sports physical.”

In an interview last month, Loft said sex-verification requirements created additional barriers for girls to participate in athletics, noting they were already twice as likely as boys to drop out of sports by age 14: “I don’t see this as a way to level the playing field for girls, and we’re making a villain out of trans girls who are children.”

Civil rights advocates have also argued that Washington’s ban was unconstitutional, violating students’ rights to privacy and equal protection rights. The initiative is due to go into effect in December, though it could face legal challenges.

title: Burnham says long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed until January – as it happened
excerpt:
The document has been described as the core policy statement coming from No 10

Andy Burnham has confirmed that his long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed.

In his speech outside No 10 on the day he...
body_text:
The document has been described as the core policy statement coming from No 10

Andy Burnham has confirmed that his long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed.

In his speech outside No 10 on the day he became PM, Burham declared that “later this year” he would “bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan, laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be”. The document has been described as the core policy statement coming from No 10 this year, with some insiders briefing that the budget was relatively low-key because key announcements were being held back for the 10-year plan.

But we may have to wait a little longer then expected until we see it. In an interview with Hugo Gye from the Economist, when asked when it would appear, Burnham said:

double quotation markWe may go into the new year, to be honest ... December or January, I think we will need to leave that open.

Burnham was speaking after Ailbhe Rea in the New Statesman published an article yesterday suggesting that, even when the initial 10-year plan announcement comes at the end of this year (or in January), that won’t be the final word. Rea said:

double quotation markYet, with expectations high, some familiar with the process are already worried that the Ten-Year Plan may be another kicking of the can. I can reveal that it may not be the long, comprehensive document that we might have expected, and will be the beginning – not the end – of a long consultation process.

It will be a speech, delivered by the prime minister before Christmas, to tick the box of a plan delivered “later this year”, accompanied by a document that may be “slimmer than expected”. It will mark the beginning of a six-to-nine-month process of consulting with the public, think tanks and everybody else about government priorities – as well as kickstarting work across government to define what some of its plans will look like in more detail. That process, in turn, will set the priorities for the spending review, itself a procedure that will take months. Suddenly, critics fear, we are looking at a government spending well over a year discussing its plans without taking the major action to address them.

Andy Burnham has said he wants to “recast” the UK’s deal to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington, which said the agreement could instead be modelled on America’s Greenland deal with Denmark.

Andy Burnham has confirmed that his long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed. (See 12.42pm.)

Shabana Mahmood’s changes to the migration system could harm women and children, a Labour MP has warned, as members of her own party continue to raise concerns with the home secretary’s proposals.

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.

For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has said her officials are “extremely excited” about one of the more obscure, but potentially most significant, changes in last week’s budget – the creation of a new category of “preventative” spending.

Internal government spending negotiations are all about DEL (departmental expenditure limits), and standard government accounting differentiates between resource DEL (day-to-day spending) and capital DEL.

Last week John Healey, the chancellor, announced that he would create a new category of ringfenced spending in the spending review next year – preventative DEL, or PDEL. This will ensure that budgets are protected for measures involving early intervention to create savings in the long term.

Giving evidence to the Commons health committee yesterday, Cooper said that her public health officials were “extremely excited” about this announcement. She said:

double quotation markWe think a lot of our investment across not just public health but across the NHS has benefits in terms of keeping people healthy and in work. A lot of those treatment budgets have a consequence in helping people work as well as in the direct prevention.

Cooper said that, as a former Treasury minister, she knew that preventative programmes designed to deliver benefits in the long term were “the areas that always come under shortest-term pressure”.

Asked how rigorous her definition of preventative spending would be, she replied:

double quotation markMine would be quite broad; we do not yet know what the Treasury’s will be …

A lot of our treatment services have an impact, in saving money elsewhere. Mental health is a really good example, as we know that a lot of young people who are not in work could benefit from mental health support.

Cooper is already in a better position than most other cabinet ministers because the health budget is one of the few that it nominally protected from real-terms cuts.

Heather Stewart, the Guardian’s economics editor, wrote a good column on the potential benefits of PDEL at the weekend.

Peter Walker has also posted these on Bluesky about what Angus MacIntyre said when Peter asked him why he did not mention Ukraine in his first speech as Reform UK’s armed forces spokesperson.

double quotation markIn a 16-minute speech on defence, Reform’s new armed forces spokesperson did not mention Ukraine or Iran once.

double quotation markWorth noting that I asked MacIntyre about this after and he said this was simply as his speech was to introduce him and his role, and that Ukraine/Iran are very much a focus

Peter Walker is a senior Guardian political correspondent.
 
 
 Polling numbers which have seen the Conservatives climb above Reform UK are not credible, Nigel Farage has said, claiming that there had been “jiggery-pokery” intended to restore the two-party system.

Farage made the claim unprompted while speaking to reporters after a speech when he was asked if Reform UK had failed in vetting, given the number of councillors and candidates found to have said offensive things or, in some cases, charged with serious offences.

The Reform UK leader said that while politicians from other parties had been arrested for alleged offences, it was only those connected to his party – notably this week’s charging of George Madgwick, its leader on Hampshire county council, with 12 counts of rape and other offences – that led to “a BBC push notification – the others don’t”.

double quotation markWhat I will tell you is this: the jiggery-pokery that is going on with polling is utterly astonishing. And if you believe the polls you’ve seen this week, you’re not understanding what’s going on out there. On the raw data, we’re four points higher, and the Conservatives are nearly four points lower than the reality.

And I know there’s a desperate push from the establishment – let’s get back to two-party politics, let’s get back to Tweedledum and Tweedledee. Let’s get back to total failure. Let’s make sure there’s no change.

It simply isn’t true. What you’ve seen from the polling industry is nonsense, and I mean that.

He did not offer any evidence for the claim.

Farage adopted a different line in a recent GB News appearance when he said he did not mind being behind in the opinion polls because he thought that would make campaigning easier. (See 1.51pm.)

Peter Walker is a senior Guardian political correspondent.

The main lesson for Reform UK from the Republicans’ huge defeat in the US midterm elections is “keep your promises”, Nigel Farage has told reporters in his first comments since the results.

Speaking after a media event at which the party unveiled their new armed forces spokesperson, Angus MacIntyre, a former RAF officer, Farage said Trump was also being punished for the “bizarre” decision to wage a long-term conflict with Iran.

Asked if he had learned something from the US results, Farage said:

double quotation markYes, keep your promises. Trump was very good in the first term and the second term in keeping his promises, but he broke a promise. That was no more foreign wars, and we’re eight months in, and the resultant rise in gas and diesel prices, more than anything else, is what did them in.

The key focus must be keeping your promises, and the cost of living, of course.

Asked if the Iran war – which Farage did not initially oppose – was a mistake, Farage said:

double quotation markNo question about it. I mean, to have quick tactical strikes from Diego Garcia, to try and maybe not halt, but at least slow the nuclear weapons programme, I totally agree with that …

But would I have said to them, ‘Yes, come on, let’s go to war for the next eight months or three years’? No, of course not. And that is so bizarre.

The government has announced it is spending £13m on another wave of Valour-recognised support centres for military veterans and their families. In the first round, 14 organisations got funding earlier this year, and another 21 organisations are now getting money. “An estimated one million veterans and their families in the UK will benefit from easier access to local services, thanks to the Valour network expanding,” the government says.

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of causing “distress and uncertainty” to hundreds of thousands of refugees by quietly introducing plans to force them to wait up to 30 years before being granted the right to settle in the UK, Rajeev Syal reports.

The latest episode of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey talking about the US midterm elections results, and what lessons they may offer to Labour.

After MacIntyre finished his speech, Farage did not take questions on camera in the main hall where the rally was taking place. But he is speaking to journalists in a “huddle” shortly.

MacIntyre says, if Reform UK wins the election, it will end ongoing prosections of veterans.

And future prosecutions would only be allowed with the consent of the defence secretary, he says.

(This is not that different from the situation that will apply under the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, currently going through parliament. It says any Troubles-related prosecutions will only be allowed with the explicit consent of the attorney general.)

MacIntyre complains about the prosecution of veterans over alleged war crimes. Veterans should be treated as heroes, but they are treated as criminals, he says.

double quotation markHuman rights lawyers dissect the decisions taken by servicemen in the heat of battle, life and death situations that no civilian can imagine.

Government lawyers use the luxury of hindsight, often decades on, to drag our veterans through the courts, treating them as criminals at every stage.

We are witnessing the Marxist rewriting of history’s narratives, calling evil good and good evil.

A functioning society celebrates, not criminalises, its armed forces personnel.

My colleague Peter Walker is at the Reform UK event. He has posted these about Angus MacIntyre.

double quotation markI am at a Reform UK event at which they are about to unveil their new armed forces [spokesperson], a just-retired RAF officer called Angus MacIntyre. As someone who ended a 40-year military career just last week he has no apparent social media presence, which must be useful for Reform.

double quotation markNote he is armed forces spokesperson, not the main defence brief. Two years-plus from the election, that brief for Reform is still unfilled, as are a few other fairly key ones eg health.

double quotation markMacIntyre seems like a real believer. This is him on asylum: “Uncontrolled illegal migration has brought hundreds of thsouands of undocumented fighting-age males, many with combat eperience and operatives from hostile states into the heart of our communities.”

double quotation markHe also says that zet zero has “collapsed our industrial base, and they put our energy sovereignty at risk”. He is a confident speaker, so my guess is we’ll see a fair bit more of him. But he is also a complete political novice, so there is always a risk of something going wrong.

title: EU presses UK to guarantee discounted university tuition fees for European students
excerpt:
Failure to agree lower fees for EU citizens studying in UK should delay prized food and drink deal, members say

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European stu...
body_text:
Failure to agree lower fees for EU citizens studying in UK should delay prized food and drink deal, members say

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.

At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.

These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.

But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.

The EU wants a return to the pre-Brexit status quo where European students paid the UK domestic rate of university tuition, rather than international fees, which can be about four to six times higher for an undergraduate degree.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing an agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

But at least six member states, including in central and eastern Europe, want the university fees issue settled by the summit, while many are seeking a firmer commitment on the issue from the British government, according to four EU sources.

One EU diplomat told the Guardian: “Having a youth experience scheme without an agreement on tuition fees has very little added value,” noting the much lower cost of university education in many EU countries and therefore potential greater advantage to British students.

A second EU diplomat said there was cautious optimism about the November summit, but “a large majority” wanted “a more convincing British commitment” on tuition fees.

A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on leaks or provide a running commentary on live negotiations. We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”

For the EU, the creation of a youth experience scheme, known as Yes, which will enable those aged 18 to 30 to live, work and study on both sides of the Channel is a high priority. The erosion of people-to-people links is seen as one of the big losses of Brexit, and many European officials studied in the UK, making the issue especially resonant.

EU officials argue the bloc has leverage, saying the food and drink deal – a Labour manifesto pledge estimated to be worth £5.1bn a year to the British economy – would come into force only if there was a satisfactory agreement on tuition fees.

Similarly, the agreement to relink emissions trading systems sundered by Brexit, which would protect British exporters from European carbon taxes, could also be delayed pending agreement on tuition fees.

A leaked version of the summit statement hints at the link between the trio of agreements, looking forward to “their joint and timely entry into force”.

Separately, EU sources have suggested without a deal on tuition fees, the EU could delay talks on British reintegration into the European electricity market that are expected to intensify next year. To secure its return to the market, the UK would have to pledge an “appropriate” contribution to European cohesion funds aimed at boosting economic development in poorer regions.

This week the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.

The EU said there would be no deal on Made in Europe at the November summit because the bloc was still finalising its position on the key draft law, the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).

Targeted at strategic industrial sectors, such as electric cars and renewables, the law would mean public subsidies and contracts would only go towards products made in Europe.

France, supported by many lawmakers in the European parliament, is pushing for a narrow definition of Made in Europe, while Germany leads a larger group of countries that don’t want to exclude trade partners including the UK.

While Britain is keen to resolve the issue, EU lawmakers are not expected to finalise the IAA text until next spring. In a significant milestone, France and Germany struck a compromise on Made in Europe favourable to the UK, but it only applies to cars, not the other industrial sectors in the IAA such as renewables and nuclear technology, or other draft proposals aimed at promoting European preference.

In a win for the UK, the draft summit statement proposes a “trusted partnership” on strategic industries, starting with steel and defence. The aim is to stop either side becoming collateral damage of the other’s trade defence measures targeted at China’s heavily subsidised imports.

title: LeBron James sends cease and desist to 'Bron AI' sports betting app over unauthorized likeness
excerpt:
Craig Carton blasts LeBron James, Derek Jeter, and Eli Manning for a shameless cash grab in their controversial new sports gambling commercial. Plus, Daryl

LeBron James has issued a cease-and-desist ...
body_text:
Craig Carton blasts LeBron James, Derek Jeter, and Eli Manning for a shameless cash grab in their controversial new sports gambling commercial. Plus, Daryl

LeBron James has issued a cease-and-desist letter to an AI-powered sports betting tool that the NBA star says uses his likeness, a spokesperson for James confirmed.

Anish Gupta, the CEO of the app "Bron AI," released a video that features a person resembling James wearing a jersey with his nickname, "Bron," and the number 23.

The character appears to be scrolling through players before stopping on Dillon Brooks, a longtime rival of James.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James passes the ball during the second quarter against the Chicago Bulls at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia on Nov. 2, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah," the character says.

According to Apple's App Store, Bron is "a sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team brands, a multi-leg Slip, and bet tracking."

But the striking resemblance to the NBA's all-time leading scorer was enough for James himself to act.

"LeBron is in no way affiliated with this unauthorized use of his likeness," a spokesperson for James said to Front Office Sports.

The letter said the "unauthorized use and illicit exploitation of" James' "name, nickname, likeness, image, persona, and other identifying attributes, materials and related information" were used in the ad. The letter also says that it implies James is "involved with betting on basketball, which is a very serious violation of NBA rules and regulations."

LeBron James #23 of the Philadelphia 76ers looks on during the game against the Chicago Bulls on November 2, 2026 at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. NBAE (Photo by David Dow/NBAE via Getty Images) (David Dow/NBAE via Getty Images)

VICTOR WEMBANYAMA DOES BEST WILT CHAMBERLAIN IMPRESSION WITH 50-20 NIGHT, SAYS HE CAN 'STILL DO MORE'

James has a brand deal with the prediction market Polymarket.

The letter is asking Bron AI to permanently stop using James' likeness and tell everyone who uses the app that the Philadelphia 76ers star is not affiliated with the app.

"I’m sure the intent here was for us to send a cease and desist in order to make it a story," James' longtime media adviser Adam Mendelsohn told Front Office Sports. "You would prefer not to respond but you don’t have a choice in a situation like this. It’s not the first time and it won’t be the last. For what it’s worth, these gimmicks never work because people see through it."

Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James (23) in the first half against the Indiana Pacers at Gainbridge Fieldhouse. Mandatory Credit: Trevor Ruszkowski-Imagn Images (Trevor Ruszkowski-Imagn Images)

The app is free to download but costs $249.99 annually, or $29.99 monthly, to use its pro version.

title: Ukraine raises death toll from Russian strike on Zaporizhia to 40 people
excerpt:
Ukrainian authorities have raised the death toll from a Russian attack on an aid centre in the Zaporizhia region in the southeast of the country to 40 people.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced ...
body_text:
Ukrainian authorities have raised the death toll from a Russian attack on an aid centre in the Zaporizhia region in the southeast of the country to 40 people.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the raised toll on Wednesday, adding that some bodies had not yet been accounted for and that more than 30 people may still be under the rubble.

The strike on Monday was one of the deadliest strikes on civilians of Russia’s nearly five-year-long war on its neighbour. It came as Kyiv prepares to attend ceasefire talks with Moscow next week that have been brokered by the United States.

Local officials had earlier confirmed 37 deaths, adding that they estimate about 38 people could remain trapped following the attack, in which Russia dropped several bombs on a school building in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line, which was being used to distribute aid.

Ukraine said that a strike then hit an underground shelter filled with people in a follow-up attack. Four police officers and two members of a rescue crew were among the dead.

Zelenskyy condemned the “vile terrorist strike” and declared that it showed that Russia did not want de-escalation of the conflict. He added that the attack had wasted an opportunity created by a ceasefire and humanitarian mission last week in the front-line village of Oleshky.

Ukrainian police have released body-camera footage from one of the four officers killed, showing people being ushered into the underground shelter as the officer receives a radio warning of incoming guided aerial bombs.

People were then seen inside the shelter before the footage cuts to black and silence.

The United Nations human rights mission in Ukraine said on Tuesday that the bombing likely violated international law.

Local authorities said that Russian drones were hampering the search for victims in Komyshuvakha. Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the regional military administration, insisted, however, that operations would continue.

The US has announced a new round of talks aimed at ending the war for next week. Special envoy Steve Witkoff has said delegations from Ukraine and Russia will meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 to discuss post-war security agreements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures and ending the war.

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to the talks after meeting Witkoff in St Petersburg on October 21. However, previous such meetings have secured little progress, with Moscow refusing to compromise on hardline demands, including that Kyiv give up territory, demilitarise, and guarantee it will not seek to join NATO.

The Trump administration has appeared to offer support for Russia’s position, stoking concern in Kyiv and across Europe.

Zelenskyy has in the past sought to sway the US president by outlining the suffering of his country, and appeared to try to repeat the trick concerning the Zaporizhia atrocity.

“Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack,” the Ukrainian president said in a social media post. “But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”

title: Under threat of air strikes, US looks to bolster base infrastructure with 3D printing
excerpt:
With many U.S. bases in the Middle East damaged by Iranian bombardment, the U.S. Air Force wants to develop mobile 3D concrete printers to erect buildings quickly.

“Put bluntly, the Air Force has spe...
body_text:
With many U.S. bases in the Middle East damaged by Iranian bombardment, the U.S. Air Force wants to develop mobile 3D concrete printers to erect buildings quickly.

“Put bluntly, the Air Force has spent decades building exquisite kill chains while too often housing the airmen who sustain them in tents, trailers, and flat-walled structures that were never designed for the threat environment now arriving overhead,” admitted the Air Force’s Small Business Innovation Research solicitation, which will close in January 2027.

Concrete printing, in which printers deposit layers of material to form structures, is gaining traction in commercial construction. The Air Force already used 3D printing to rebuild hurricane-damaged Tyndall Air Force Base, Florida, in 2023, while a Maryland Air National Guard civil engineer squadron is developing its own mobile concrete printer.

But the new SBIR, which is a direct-to-Phase II project, suggests the Air Force wants 3D construction capability imminently. The goal is to enable “military engineers to rapidly print protective structures using automated or semi-automated construction workflows, reduced skilled labor, and locally available cementitious materials where feasible,” the Air Force said.

While 3D concrete printers exist, the Air Force is concerned that the technology is not yet ready to build structures that can survive bombardment by missiles and drones. Hundreds of U.S. military buildings across eight Middle Eastern countries were damaged by Iranian attacks, according to a September 2026 report by the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General.

The problem is that “the existing state of the art has not yet fully addressed the combined problem that matters most for combat survivability: printable expeditionary materials, field-executable operator workflows, and structure geometry deliberately optimized to mitigate blast-wave behavior and fragmentation effects,” said the SBIR.

The project will evaluate cement-like materials for qualities such as strength, adhesion and the availability of local components. It will develop new construction geometries “that improve survivability beyond conventional flat-wall construction, including shapes intended to reduce blast reflection, limit pressure amplification, interrupt fragmentation paths, and improve internal occupant protection.”

Ultimately, the Air Force wants a mobile concrete printer that can quickly and consistently erect structures while being operated “in austere conditions by lightly trained military personnel.”

The Air Force foresees “substantial” dual-use applications for the mobile concrete printers, such as critical infrastructure and humanitarian relief. However, the SBIR also notes that commercialization will likely require numerous approvals in areas such as building codes.

The aim is to “transition the capability from ‘we can print something interesting’ to ‘a civil engineer unit can deploy, set up, print, inspect, and use protective infrastructure fast enough to matter,’” the service said.
