Oakland, California – Protesters dressed as cardboard robots chanted and danced to a drumbeat as they protested against new data centres outside Oakland City Hall last month.

Their concerns largely focused on how the centres — which process large amounts of digital information — might strain the energy grid.

The result, they argued, would not only be environmental harm but also sky-high electricity bills for local households.

“Power prices have gone up so much in Oakland that some people are thinking of shutting off their power,” said Carlos Gutierrez, an activist for Communities for a Better Environment, an environmental justice group.

“And the city is planning to provide power to a data centre instead.”

Opposition to data centres is growing across the United States, as residents express concern about their rapid expansion.

More than 3,000 data centres already operate in the country, with more than 1,500 others in development, according to the Pew Research Center.

But the backlash is perhaps most striking in California’s San Francisco Bay Area, a region considered to be the heart of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

Major AI companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta are based in the Bay Area, and the industry’s growth has been credited with fuelling a local economic renaissance.

Data centres house the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run AI-powered services such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

But they also require 24-hour power and a large supply of water to cool their processors.

Even with such cooling technology, data centres are notorious for emitting heat, leading to an increase in land surface temperatures as high as 9 degrees Celsius (16 degrees Fahrenheit).

Concerns about the cost of rapid data centre growth, both environmentally and financially, have catapulted the issue into the discourse around Tuesday’s midterm elections.

In the final two months before the vote, at least seven Bay Area cities, including San Francisco and Richmond, have passed temporary moratoriums on data centre construction.

They include Oakland, which passed a data centre moratorium on October 6, after days of protest.

Local politicians competing in Tuesday’s midterms have also used the topic as a wedge issue, to rally support among certain pockets of voters.

One of the most closely watched races in the Bay Area is for the seat left vacant by longtime Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi. After 39 years in the House of Representatives, Pelosi is retiring at the end of the year.

Two Democrats are competing in Tuesday’s election to fill her position in Congress: San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and state Senator Scott Wiener.

Each one has staked out a different position on AI data centres. Wiener, for instance, opposes any ban on data centres.

“A blanket data centre moratorium could undermine AI regulation,” he told the publication Mission Local.

Chan, meanwhile, has pledged to seek a nationwide moratorium on data centres, at least until responsible AI regulation is put in place.

“Let’s start with a moratorium on data centres. Allow us to have that moment to regulate artificial intelligence,” she said at a debate in October.

Chan played a leading role in passing San Francisco’s moratorium in early October.

A poll from the University of Southern California showed Wiener leading Chan 47 percent to 41, as of mid-October.

“Right now, data centre opposition is an issue that unifies the US public like no other,” said Shum Preston, a political analyst based in San Francisco.

So far, there has been relatively little opposition to the data centre moratoriums in local hearings. But he speculates that there may be several reasons for the lack of pushback to the bans.

Among them are the surveys indicating widespread public backlash to data centre creation.

An October CNBC poll found that 63 percent of registered US voters oppose building data centres within 16 kilometres, or 10 miles, of their homes.

“Data centres poll very poorly, and developers probably don’t want to put their supervisor friends in trouble ahead of elections. So they probably let this pass,” Preston said.

He also signalled that the short-term nature of the moratoriums may be a factor.

Certain Bay Area cities like San Francisco, Brisbane and Oakland paused construction on data centres for 45 days, with the option to extend the ban later.

Opponents of the moratoriums “will be more vocal when” the 45 days end, Preston said. By that time, the heat of the midterm election season will also have settled, he added.

“That’s when the hearings will get more contentious,” he said.

Another hurdle facing the moratoriums is the lack of transparency surrounding data centre construction.

Supervisor Shamann Walton, who sponsored San Francisco’s moratorium ordinance, has argued that the city’s definition of “data centres” is outdated.

Created in 2001 — long before the AI boom — the city planning code defines data centres as “internet service exchanges”, a definition that may not accurately characterise the technology today.

Walton said the outdated language has made it hard for authorities to count how many data centres exist in the city.

Not being able to identify data centres can also prevent city officials from monitoring their power and water usage.

“We cannot use 2001 rules to regulate 2026 technology,” he said in a September 14 statement.

Another issue is the time it takes to carry out the necessary environmental assessments. The moratoriums may not offer enough time for a comprehensive review.

“Forty-five days is hardly enough time to document and study the impacts and then frame regulations,” said Roger Lin, senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, a US environmental nonprofit.

He added that legal barriers limit access to such information from the data centres themselves.

“Data centres often have nondisclosure agreements, so even local air quality boards may not know the impact of data centres on air quality,” said Lin.

Still, AI industry supporters have touted the growth of the data centres as evidence of a flourishing industry, with positive downstream effects for US communities.

Anthropic, for instance, is preparing an initial public offering (IPO) that is likely to raise billions of dollars.

But critics warn that the company’s growth may not translate into an economic boom for the San Francisco Bay Area overall.

Instead, residents fear unequal economic growth that primarily benefits the wealthy. Already, San Francisco faces some of the highest and fastest-growing home rental prices in the country.

At a hearing at San Francisco City Hall, a resident vented their frustrations about the data centres to the supervisors.

“This city is less for humans and more for robots and billionaires,” the resident said.

title: Israeli forces kill four in Gaza as fifth Palestinian dies of wounds
excerpt:
Israeli forces have killed at least four Palestinians in attacks across Gaza, while a fifth person died of wounds sustained in an earlier assault, according to medical sources and media reports.

At l...
body_text:
Israeli forces have killed at least four Palestinians in attacks across Gaza, while a fifth person died of wounds sustained in an earlier assault, according to medical sources and media reports.

At least two people were killed in a gun attack and an air raid on southern Khan Younis on Monday, while a third was killed in a drone attack on the central al-Musaddar village, medical sources said.

The fourth person died in a strike on a vehicle in northern Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, according to the Wafa news agency. It identified the victim as Hani Hamed Kahil and said five others were wounded in the attack.

The Israeli military said it targeted Palestinian fighters in three strikes, but provided no further details.

Wafa reported that a fifth person, Youssef Abu Younis, also died of injuries sustained in an Israeli attack on a police post in al-Mawasi on Sunday. His death brought the number of deaths reported on Monday to five.

Earlier, at least five Palestinian police officers were killed in an attack on Sunday.

Elsewhere in Gaza City, three Palestinians were wounded on Monday when a minibus belonging to a community kitchen was hit in Zeitoun.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,593 Palestinians since the United States-brokered “ceasefire” began in October 2025, and wounded 5,748 others. Overall, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,609 Palestinians and wounded 175,872 people.

The latest attacks came amid efforts to secure shelter for displaced Palestinians before winter.

Israeli Army Radio reported that Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative of the Board of Peace, established by the US to oversee a so-called peace plan in Gaza, arrived in Israel on Monday to seek permission to bring in tents and push for steps to accelerate reconstruction.

The scale of the need in Gaza remains vast. The United Nations migration agency said on October 9 that nearly two million people required shelter assistance and half of Gaza’s tents and makeshift shelters needed replacing, leaving families exposed as winter approached.

title: Mamdani threatens to sue Trump admin over ICE's use of city-owned lots for immigration enforcement
excerpt: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday labeled U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "cruel" as Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the city does not "coordinate" with ICE, ahead of this w...
body_text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday labeled U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "cruel" as Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the city does not "coordinate" with ICE, ahead of this weekend's gatherings.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) reported use of city-owned parking lots to stage immigration enforcement operations without the city's authorization.

In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani said he is "deeply troubled" by reports of ICE agents "using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations," which the mayor said is unauthorized and illegal.

"This use of City property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property," Mamdani wrote in the letter. "If your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property."

DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani threatened to sue the Trump administration over ICE's alleged use of city property to stage immigration enforcement operations. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

According to the mayor's letter, ICE agents have reportedly parked their vehicles and conducted meetings in several city-owned, unstaffed parking lots, including in a parking lot at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx as well as in parking lots along 111th Street on the west side of Flushing Meadows Corona Park in Queens, which is located next to a city-run preschool and several cultural institutions welcome hundreds of children and families every day.

"ICE has not secured any authorization from the City to use these lots for immigration enforcement. To be clear: the City does not authorize ICE using its property in this manner," Mamdani wrote.

"Parking lots connected to City parks are reserved for the safe use and enjoyment of New Yorkers and visitors who wish to use our parks," he continued. "Use of these lots for other purposes, including ICE’s reported use of these lots, amounts to unauthorized activity on City property. Accordingly, you must immediately issue guidance to your agents prohibiting them from using any City lots to stage or conduct enforcement operations."

Mamdani added that New York City "deeply values its immigrant communities and will continue to use all available lawful means to ensure their safety, well-being, and ability to navigate the City and its resources without fear."

MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION'

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he is "deeply troubled" by reports of ICE agents "using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations." (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Last month, Mamdani and other New York Democratic leaders pushed for the city’s private parking lot owners to ban ICE from their properties.

"In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations," the mayor wrote in a letter to property owners and operators.

MAMDANI SAYS EVEN IF HE CAN GET ALONG WITH TRUMP, HE STILL DEMANDS THAT 'ICE SHOULD BE ABOLISHED'

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has previously pushed for ICE to be abolished. (Christopher Dilts/Getty Images)

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., were among more than 100 elected officials who signed on to Mamdani's October letter.

Mamdani has previously pushed for ICE to be abolished, including after an ICE agent shot and killed Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston in July and after another ICE agent shot and wounded Dominican national Oscar Belgal during an enforcement operation in New York City last month.

title: What time do polls open and close in the US midterm elections 2026?
excerpt:
Why the US midterms matter even if you don't live in America

More than 230 million eligible voters across the United States can head to the polls on Tuesday to decide who will represent them in Congr...
body_text:
Why the US midterms matter even if you don't live in America

More than 230 million eligible voters across the United States can head to the polls on Tuesday to decide who will represent them in Congress.

All 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested. Voters in 36 states will also elect governors. Republicans currently hold both chambers.

Voting hours are determined and set by each state.

The first polls are set to open in Vermont at 5am (10:00 GMT). Voting in New Jersey, Virginia, Connecticut and Kentucky will start at 6am (11:00 GMT).

Voting in Georgia, Florida, Pennsylvania and New York will start between 6am (11:00 GMT) and 7am (12:00 GMT), while Ohio and North Carolina will see voting start at 6:30am (11:30 GMT).

In Michigan, polls will open at 7am (12:00 GMT).

Polls close in waves across the country, with the earliest closures at 6pm (23:00 GMT) in Indiana and Kentucky.

Voting in Michigan closes at 8pm and in Kansas at 7pm local time (both 01:00 GMT on Wednesday), while polls in Iowa close at 8pm (02:00 GMT on Wednesday).

Alaska is the last to close, at around 1am Eastern Time (06:00 GMT) on Wednesday.

The first results could start arriving on Tuesday as polls begin to close.

Results will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening, and some on Wednesday as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts.

However, the first reported results will not necessarily mean that a winner has been announced.

Election officials release vote counts as ballots are processed, while news organisations such as the Associated Press analyse the results and determine when a race can be called.

Closely contested races could take hours, or even days, to call. It might not be immediately clear which party will control Congress.

Voters can cast their ballots by mail, early or in person on election day, which is Tuesday.

Many mail, provisional and other ballots are counted after election night, which is why tallies can take a few days, or even weeks, to finalise.

Senate Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a majority. House Democrats need three seats for a majority.

title: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
excerpt:
Al Jazeera investigation exposes paramilitary hitman linked to Turning Point UK

The United Kingdom has revised its immigration rules, doubling the time most foreign workers must wait to qualify for p...
body_text:
Al Jazeera investigation exposes paramilitary hitman linked to Turning Point UK

The United Kingdom has revised its immigration rules, doubling the time most foreign workers must wait to qualify for permanent residency to 10 years and making refugees who arrive on “small boats” wait as long as 30 years.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, speaking in Parliament on Monday, said hundreds of thousands of care workers will be exempt from the hardline rules, offering a concession amid a political outcry within the governing Labour Party.

Permanent residency, known in the UK as indefinite leave to remain, carries the right to work, study, use the free National Health Service and claim welfare benefits. Until now, it has been granted after five years.

The new rules, set to take effect next year, tie eligibility for permanent residency to income.

People who earn more than 50,000 pounds a year ($67,000) will still be able to apply after five years, and those earning more than 125,000 pounds ($167,500) after three. Everyone else will be placed on the 10-year path. The median salary in the UK is about 39,000 pounds (roughly $52,000).

The rules will apply retroactively to workers already in the country.

“Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Mahmood, the home secretary, told Parliament, adding that the changes would restore fairness by linking the right to settle to what immigrants contribute.

“Those who contribute most will settle fastest,” she said. “Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait longer.”

The UK government first proposed last year that lower-skilled workers wait 10 to 15 years for permanent residency.

But the plan drew fierce opposition from unions and parts of the Labour Party, particularly over its effect on care workers, who are often poorly paid and work in a sector that has long struggled to fill vacancies. Many of them arrived in the early 2020s, as the country was reeling from the COVID-19 pandemic, to fill gaps left by European workers who had departed after Brexit.

Under the revised plan, care workers will be able to settle after five years if they have met the conditions of their visas and earn at least 25,000 pounds ($33,500) a year.

Mahmood said the rules would offer a path for care workers “who worked hard and answered our call when we needed them”.

As for refugees, those who arrive through one of the government’s “new safe and legal routes” will be able to settle after five years, she said. For other refugees, the standard wait will become 20 years, reduced to 10 years for those who work or study. Anyone who arrived by an “illegal method”, such as by small boat, could wait up to 30 years for settlement, she said.

Under the new rules, applicants will also be disqualified if they have a criminal record, cannot speak English “to a high standard”, owe money to the government, or have not made at least three years of national insurance contributions.

Mahmood said the overhaul would mean that half a million people would settle later than they otherwise would have, saving the government billions of pounds in benefits.

In total, the government estimates that as many as 1.4 million people will receive settled status between 2026 and 2030.

The changes, announced after a 12-week public consultation that drew more than 200,000 responses, are part of a broader effort to tighten immigration rules after arrivals surged following Brexit.

They are a response to political pressure, including from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK party, which has surged in popularity in recent years with calls for stricter migration controls. Reform UK has sought to depict the arrivals of refugees on small boats across the English Channel as a crisis, and anti-immigration activists have staged protests, including outside facilities that house asylum seekers.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has said that increased law enforcement cooperation between the UK and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 percent compared with 2025.

title: Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
excerpt:
Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crash

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will investigate  whether parts of a jet that crashed in Florida broke off before it nose...
body_text:
Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crash

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will investigate  whether parts of a jet that crashed in Florida broke off before it nose-dived and exploded, killing all nine people on board.

The Learjet 60, which was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas on Sunday, crashed on a street nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.

A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died.

The NTSB said on Monday that it would also investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have been contributing factors.

Final moments before deadly Florida plane crash

It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.

"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.

NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.

The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."

The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash but that determining its probable cause will be a "lengthy investigatory process".

Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time.

Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.

As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.

Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the safety board.

Officials describe how Learjet flight unfolded before deadly crash

Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.

In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit appears to be "we're out of time".

The seven people killed who were travelling as passengers were identified in a joint statement from their families as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma and Charlie - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.

The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.

As well as those killed, one man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the plane nosedived onto the street.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants.

Images from the crash scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.

The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.

Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash.

Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
excerpt:
A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise less than 50km (31 miles) from the Russian border in Finland

Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multina...
body_text:
A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise less than 50km (31 miles) from the Russian border in Finland

Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.

Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.

Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.

But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.

Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.

Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.

The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.

Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".

Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.

He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."

Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.

He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".

Ukrainian troops take part in urban warfare training at a military base in England in 2023

Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.

Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.

Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.

Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.

As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.

However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.

In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.

Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.

It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.

Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.

Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked

Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends

Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city

title: Trump loses supreme court bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots as justices refuse to take up emergency request – live
excerpt:
Ruling was latest judicial rebuke of unprecedented efforts from Trump administration to intervene in elections process of multiple states

Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force Californi...
body_text:
Ruling was latest judicial rebuke of unprecedented efforts from Trump administration to intervene in elections process of multiple states

Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force California to set aside ballots

The US supreme court on Monday quickly rejected the Trump administration’s request to force California to set aside thousands of mail ballots from people President Donald Trump’s administration claims are noncitizens, the Associated Press reports.

The high court refused to intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state’s voter rolls. The decision came just hours after the administration asked the supreme court to intervene.

The ruling was the latest judicial rebuke in the face of a wave of unprecedented efforts from the Trump administration to intervene in the elections process of multiple states. The midterm elections are expected to bring nationwide victories for Democrats and impose more Congressional checks on Trump’s power.

In California, the Trump administration had asked the high court to set aside the challenged ballots until the voters’ citizenship status could be verified. But officials there said that the list appeared to be filled with errors and that setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters.

The high court did not detail its reasoning for rejecting the Trump administration’s request, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.

The Cook Political Report is now predicting that Michigan’s furiously contested senate race is more likely to be won by Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, after previously categorizing it as a “toss-up” race that was too close to call.

The shift comes amid last-minute outrage as sitting Democratic Michigan congresswoman Hayley Stevens endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, despite Stevens’ previous public attacks on Rogers when during a Democratic primary election that she lost. Stevens and El-Sayed’s contrasting policy views on Israel are seen as central to a “betrayal” that many Democrats are arguing may have cost the 43-year-old Stevens her career as a Democratic politician.

Two losses in two courts in just three hours.

Judges across the country have repeatedly rebuked the Trump administration for its last-minute demand that California set aside 20,000 ballots that the administration claims it has evidence were cast by noncitizens —an unprecedented and possibly unconstitutional attempt to interfere with a state’s electoral process.

Today, the administration’s California gambit was rejected by two different courts in two separate cases in a matter of hours.

First, a federal judge in Washington ordered the Trump administration to stop demanding that California election officials set aside ballots from 20,000 people, writing, “The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone.”

Then, in a separate case, the supreme court swiftly rejected the Trump administration’s emergency request this morning that it intervene on the day before the election and force California election officials to set aside the 20,000 mail ballots.

Democratic elections attorney Marc Elias called the supreme court ruling “A complete DEFEAT for Trump DOJ” noting that the court’s denial of the administration’s request came with “no noted dissents,” even from more conservative justices, and that the court “denied DOJ’s application about the California election without even asking for us to respond.”

The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.

Extreme weather is having an impact on voting and elections in the Southwest, as the National Weather Service estimated up to four inches of rain could fall through Monday across the Four Corners region — where New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah meet — as the phenomenon stoked by warming Pacific waters known as El Niño disrupts weather patterns, the Associated Press reports.

Officials had warned of “potentially catastrophic” flooding in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town of about 2,000 nearly wiped out in 1911 when the San Juan River crested at approximately 17.8 feet (5.4 meters). The river reached 16.81 feet (5.1 meters) late Sunday night, flooding downtown streets, before receding Monday, the weather service said.

The Colorado Secretary of State’s office arranged alternative voting plans for evacuated or stranded residents of Pagosa Springs, Colorado. Other elections officials had urged voters to cast ballots before the storms hit.

Evacuations also were ordered along the San Juan River in New Mexico, which officials warned was still rising and could crest Tuesday through Wednesday. The village of Chama, New Mexico, was also evacuated and cut off by road closures.

In Michigan, where he is fighting for one of the country’s most fiercely contested US senate seats, Adbul El-Sayed and his supporters are focusing their closing message on the country’s healthcare crisis.

Speaking to reporters, El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who previously served as a county public health director, said that Medicaid coverage would be his number one priority if he his elected to the senate.

People who lose Medicaid coverage end up getting care in emergency rooms, where it is most expensive, and hospitals then push those costs into negotiations with insurers, El-Sayed said. And the cost ultimately lands on everyone, he added.

Earlier, Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, who is campaigning in Michigan for El-Sayed, told his supporters in Royal Oak, a suburb of Detroit, that that higher wages and universal healthcare must be the heart of the Democratic agenda. “We want Medicare for All,” Warren said.

Former President Barack Obama has posted his personal endorsement of Democratic candidates running in four key swing states: Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Maine.

His posts included photos of him campaigning with Democratic candidates at rallies in Georgia, Ohio, and Michigan, and a campaign video about Troy Jackson, the Democratic senate candidate in Maine.

Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat locked in an extremely close mayoral race with a challenger running to her left, Nithya Raman, has issued a statement condemning the Trump administration’s emergency appeal to the supreme court, asking for it to intervene in its attempt to force California to set aside 20,000 ballots that the administration has asserted were possibly submitted by noncitizens:

double quotation markDonald Trump is asking the supreme court to intervene in the California ballot case the day before Election Day, after lower courts have already said no. This is a desperate attempt to scare people into staying home, and it’s a distraction from the real issues that matter to Angelenos and Californians.

It’s also an effort to make Americans doubt our elections, which are safe, secure, and run by dedicated election workers. Don’t fall for it.

The Cook Political Report has released its final predictions for the likely outcome of House races, with an additional five house districts shifting more firmly towards the Democratic candidates, compared with previous estimates, election analyst Dave Wasserman wrote.

Overall, the report predicts that Democrats “will win 15 to 25 states, putting them at a 230 to 240-seat majority,” Erin Covey writes.

The five districts that Cook now sees as a bit more likely to be won by Democrats are:

Tennessee’s 9th district, where Democrat Justin Pearson, a gun violence prevention advocate, is running against Republican Brent Taylor, who is facing 11th hour questions about his alleged history of texting unsolicited nude photos

Virginia’s 5th district, where Democrat Tom Perriello is challenging incumbent Republican John McGuire

Florida’s 4th district, where Democrat LaShona Holloway is challenging incumbent Republican Aaron Bean

North Carolina’s 7th district, where Democrat Kimberly Hardy is challenging incumbent Republican David Rouzer and North Carolina’s 14th district, where Democrat Lakesha Hudson is challenging Republican Tim Moore

Abdul El Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, told over 300 supporters in Royal Oak on Monday that Republicans’ Islamophobic attacks against him were an attempt to distract voters from the policies driving up their costs.

“In MAGA terms, whenever they’re trying to distract you, it’s because they’re picking your pocket,” El Sayed said.

He argued that Donald Trump and JD Vance would rather talk about him than about the price of gas and groceries or how people can afford to see a doctor, and he mocked his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, as an “NPC,” or non-player character.

El Sayed blamed the administration’s war in Iran, its tariff fight with Canada and its health policies for rising costs and higher premiums, speaking a day before the midterm elections in the Detroit suburb.

He finished by saying that Michiganders take differences in a name or in prayer as an invitation to talk. “Royal Oak, when they come for us, we won’t back down,” he said.

A federal judge on Monday ordered the Trump administration to stop demanding that California election officials set aside ballots from 20,000 people the Department of Justice says might be noncitizens, the Associated Press reports.

The ruling by James Boasberg, a federal judge in the District of Columbia, is the latest loss for the Trump administration in its push to force California to separate ballots from people on a list of possible noncitizens. California officials say the demand comes too close to the election, with millions of ballots already cast, and that the list is riddled with errors and likely contains many US citizens.

Boasberg ruled that the administration’s demands to California violate the US constitution.

“The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” wrote Boasberg, who is based in Washington.

Boasberg’s order came just hours after the administration asked the US supreme court to intervene and issue a “limited injunction” that would direct California to set aside the ballots while a separate, but related case, US v California, plays out in court.

In that case, a district court judge had forcefully denied the Justice Department’s request to California and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in Tuesday’s midterm elections to determine control of Congress.

The Trump administration’s emergency appeal to the supreme court came after a divided appeals also court rejected the request to set aside the 20,000 ballots.

The day before the midterm elections, Trump posted a video on X reiterating his pledge to give $5,000 “all adult citizens in the United States of America” if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate.

“If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket,” Trump said in the video clip.

Trump’s claim of paying out $5,000 per person for political victory for his party has been sparking bipartisan shock and condemnation since he first suggested it in September, prompting accusations that Trump is trying to buy votes, not from a subset of swing voters, but from the entire US electorate.

The cost of a theoretical payout of that size is estimated at $1.2tn.

Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who said she would now back the Republican nominee for US Senate in Michigan, defended her decision in an interview today. The representative who has faced fierce backlash for her eleventh-hour defection, also rejected any notion that she was “forced” into her decision to pull her endorsement and support Mike Rogers, the former GOP congressman. “This is what happens to women,” Stevens told conservative commentator Scott Jennings. “Any notion that I was forced into my decision is all more of the same.”

Meanwhile, El-Sayed’s campaign announced that it received $2.4m in donations on Sunday, the day that Stevens announced she would now support Rogers. El-Sayed’s campaign that the amount is a single-day fundraising record for his Senate bid. His staff also noted that more than 26,000 people contributed for the first time on Sunday.

A day before the midterm elections, the justice department has asked the supreme court to force Califronia election officials to set aside 20,000 mail ballots, that the administration claims were submitted by non-citizens. Last week, a federal judge declined to order California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people the Trump administration claimed were non-citizens, rebuffing a legally thin request from the justice department that appeared designed to cast doubt over the results of the midterms.

As we bring you the latest polling and predictions ahead of Tuesday’s election, one notable shift is in Louisiana – where a Democrat hasn’t won a US Senate seat since 2008. Republican Julia Letlow, a Trump-backed congresswoman who beat the incumbent Bill Cassidy in her primary, will face Jamie Davis, a Democrat and third-generation farmer. Sabato’s Crystal Ball has moved the Senate race in the Pelican state from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican” – a sign that the Davis might be diluting Letlow’s strength. One of the country’s leading election forecasters, Crystal Ball also moved several of their “toss up” races to “leans Democratic”. This includes the key Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Texas and Ohio.

Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who said she would now back the Republican nominee for US Senate in Michigan, defended her decision in an interview with conservative commentator Scott Jennings today.

“I gave him an opportunity to the Senate nominee here in in Michigan to unite around something that everyone can agree on, and then I got disinvited instead,” Stevens said, referring to her comments last week where she said any appearance alongside Abdul El-Sayed was preconditioned on his denouncing an outside group’s campaign ad that had blamed US support of Israel for the rising cost of living.

El-Sayed declined the request, accusing Stevens of needlessly reopening debates from a settled primary. His campaign subsequently disinvited Stevens from a campaign event scheduled for this past weekend. El-Sayed also condemned the ad, saying that he did “not agree with its contents”.

“This is what happens to women,” Stevens said in the interview. “Any notion that I was forced into my decision is all more of the same.”

double quotation markI made a decision, and you know what? I’m hearing from a ton of people, and maybe they don’t want to come forward, but I’m hearing from a ton of people all over who are agreeing and are thanking me for just saying what I feel.

After Stevens lost the August Senate primary by a close margin in this year’s primary, she offered El-Sayed a lukewarm endorsement, but refused to openly campaign for El-Sayed for months.

Trump noted that he’d spent the last two weeks crisscossing the country, holding rallies on behalf of several embattled Republicans.

“America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote. I hope they’re ready to do the right thing,” he said, while downplaying the effects of the ongoing Iran war in a final plea to voters.

“I don’t know if you even call it a war because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. “Oil prices are plunging now. They’re plunging a record. Nobody’s ever seen a plunge like this, and they’ll be down. I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon.”

On the eve of the midterms, national average fuel prices have surged to $4.10 per gallon for gasoline – a $1.00 increase over last year – while diesel has climbed to $6.20 per gallon, nearly double its price a year ago.

Trump has now mentioned the upcoming elections, running through his greatest hits of talking points, and repeating several falsehoods in the process.

“These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up. There’s never been anything like what we’re seeing: jihadists and Muslim Brotherhood members,” he said, baselessly claiming (again) that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, is a member of the Islamist group.

Trump added that Democratic candidates are “all committed to the same radical agenda: open borders, raising your taxes by trillions of dollars, taking away your guns, transgender mutilation of your children, abolishing oil and natural gas, sending energy costs skyrocketing and opening the floodgates to millions of migrants from all over the world, hoping to get them to be able to vote”.

Donald Trump has been speaking for nearly 20 minutes, and he’s yet to actually make any substantial reference to the midterm elections which will take place tomorrow – and will decide the makeup of Congress in his final two years in office.

Instead, the president is using the opportunity to talk about his construction and makeover projects throughout Washington DC, including on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

“It’s really a beautiful thing. It’s a work of art in many ways, but it was a work of art that never worked, but now it will work,” Trump said, while joking that the pool should be renamed after him.

As we bring you the latest polling and predictions ahead of Tuesday’s election, one notable shift is in Louisiana – where a Democrat hasn’t won a US Senate seat since 2008.

Now, Republican Julia Letlow, a Trump-backed congresswoman who beat the incumbent Bill Cassidy in her primary, will face Jamie Davis, a Democrat and third-generation farmer.

Sabato’s Crystal Ball has moved the Senate race in the Pelican state from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican” – a sign that the Davis might be diluting Letlow’s strength.

One of the country’s leading election forecasters, Crystal Ball also moved several of their “toss up” races to “leans Democratic”. This includes the key Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Texas and Ohio.

Meanwhile, the forecaster also moved the competitive Iowa Senate race from “toss up” to “leans Republican”. Here, Democrat Josh Turek is attempting to beat Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson to win the open seat in the Hawkeye state.

title: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
excerpt:
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China

Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the Unit...
body_text:
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China

Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.

Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.

“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”

Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.

When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages.

The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.

Public opinion in the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.

“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”

Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.

On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.

The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. Asia was again hit harder than most. Cambodia faced a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.

After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools. In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour. In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”

Still, some analysts see a narrow opening.

Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.

That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.

Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.

“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”

Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea, where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait, which separates China from Taiwan, the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.

Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.

One area where analysts do expect some change is US policy on Chinese technology.

The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China, said Okun at APAC Advisors.

These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.

“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.

The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.

Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.

“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.

“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

title: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
excerpt:
Australian teen Noah Jones is no longer a plaintiff in the case but will attend Tuesday's hearing

Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin ...
body_text:
Australian teen Noah Jones is no longer a plaintiff in the case but will attend Tuesday's hearing

Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.

In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.

Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.

Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.

The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.

Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.

Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer.

"We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said.

"They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."

Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.

The company said it shared Australia's goal of protecting young people online "but there are better and more effective ways" than a ban.

"As we challenge this law in court, we'll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures," said Reddit's chief communications officer Adam Collins.

Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats."

"We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November.

Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.

Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.

The eSafety Commissioner - the body tasked with enforcing the ban - has launched several investigations into alleged non-compliance by Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.

WhatsApp and online gaming sites like Roblox and Discord were not included in the ban, nor were educational platforms like YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.

In the first few days of the ban, Meta - which owns three of the banned platforms - said it had closed about half a million accounts.

Some children said they were booted off their accounts in the days before and when the ban started - but many have said they were able to easily circumvent the age checks which included uploading credit card details, photo IDs or a selfie.

Australia has banned social media for kids under 16. How does it work?
